# Lua Gameplay/UI API — per-function behaviour notes

This document extends `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13 (the classic `lua_register` idiom, 1,430
individually-named engine C functions across three registrar call sites — `0x00a20840`/1,014
gameplay names, `0x008430f0`+42 wrappers/311 UI names, `0x00845aa0`/113 names). §13 established
*that* the roster exists and *where* each `{namePtr,funcPtr}` pair lives; this document decompiles
individual named entries and records their real argument signature, return value, observable side
effects, and engine subsystem, one top-level section per work item / agent pass, subsections per
function.

**Confidence labels (this project's house style):** `CONFIRMED — disassembly` (read directly from
the decompiled instruction stream — control flow, call targets, field offsets, argument-extraction
shape), `HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred` (a semantic role assigned from consistent cross-call-site
context or an argument-count/shape match against a real public API, not independently proven a
second way), `OPEN — unresolved` (a real gap — exact bitfield/enum meaning, an unresolved callee
argument count, etc.).

**Cleanroom note:** per `WALLS.md`, no raw Ghidra decompiler pseudocode expressions or auto-named
decompiler variables (`piVar8`, `iVar10`, `DAT_...`, etc.) are quoted verbatim anywhere in this
document — behaviour is described in plain English citing only function/data addresses and real,
public, documented Lua 5.1 C API names.

**Method, shared by every subsection below (established once here, not repeated per function):**
every one of this document's entries is a `lua_CFunction`-shaped routine — `int fn(lua_State *L)`
— reached by decompiling the paired function pointer recovered from `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13's
own `{namePtr,funcPtr}` array-walk method. All of them open with the same, evidently
machine-generated binding-wrapper prologue: a call to a 1-argument helper matching the real public
**`lua_gettop(L)`** (`0x00dfde50`) to read the total argument count `N`, followed by a sequence of
positional reads for the mandatory leading arguments and a **trailing-optional countdown** for any
remaining arguments (each optional argument is guarded by a nil/absence test before extraction, and
defaults to a fixed literal when absent or nil — the shape is `if (remaining < 1) use_default; else
if (is_nil_test) use_default; else extract;`, decremented once per optional argument checked, front
to back). The primitives identified and reused across this cluster:

- **`0x00dfde50`** — 1 argument (`L`) → int. Shape matches the real public **`lua_gettop`** exactly
  (only 1-argument Lua 5.1 API returning "how many values are on the stack"). Used first, in every
  function in this cluster, to obtain the real argument count. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred from
  argument-count match + universal first-call position; not independently proven a second way.]**
- **`0x00dfe210(L, idx, 0)`** — 3 arguments, third always a literal `0`. Shape matches the real
  public **`lua_tolstring(L, idx, len)`** exactly (the only 3-argument "read a value off the Lua
  stack" function in the public API; a literal `0`/`NULL` third argument is exactly how the public
  `lua_tostring` convenience macro expands `lua_tolstring(L,i,NULL)`). Every result this document
  observed being used is either kept as an opaque pointer/handle passed straight into a
  name-resolver, or used directly as a string. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred, same basis.]**
- **`0x00dfe1e0(L, idx)`** — 2 arguments → 0/1-shaped int. Shape matches the real public
  **`lua_toboolean(L, idx)`** exactly, and every result this document observed is stored into a
  `bool`-typed local. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred, same basis.]**
- **`0x00dfe040(L, idx)`** — 2 arguments → int, used only as an `==0`/`!=0` gate immediately before
  an optional-argument extraction (never itself supplying the extracted value). Shape matches the
  real public **`lua_type(L, idx)`** (2 arguments), and every call site's `==0` branch is exactly
  where the surrounding code falls through to a hard-coded default — consistent with testing the
  real Lua 5.1 `LUA_TNIL` tag value (`0`). **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred; the exact tag being tested
  is not independently re-derived against `lua_type`'s other tag constants, only against `0`.]**
- **`0x00dfe590(L, v)`** — 2 arguments, called only at the very end of the two functions in this
  cluster that end with a literal `return 1;` (the real `lua_CFunction` convention: the C return
  value is the count of Lua values pushed). Both observed call sites push a 0/1-shaped result.
  Shape matches a real public `lua_push*`-family call (most consistent with **`lua_pushboolean`**
  given the observed value shape, but not independently distinguished from `lua_pushinteger`).
  **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred.]**
- **`0x00dfe160(L, idx)` immediately followed by a zero-argument call `0x00ea2596()`** — a second,
  rarer optional-argument extractor for a numeric/flag-shaped trailing argument (seen where the
  default is a small literal such as `3` or `0`, later consumed as a bitmask, e.g. tested with
  `& 2`). `0x00ea2596` taking no visible `L` argument is inconsistent with the plain public Lua
  C API shape the rest of this list matches cleanly. ~~**[OPEN — the pair's exact real-API identity
  is not resolved; treated here only as "the flags/number extractor," not attributed to a specific
  named public function.]**~~ **RESOLVED, §4.1 ~~(also independently re-confirmed under emulation,
  §5.3 below)~~ (§5.3 emulates `0x00dab330`, not these primitives): `0x00dfe160` is the real public `lua_tonumber(L, idx)`; `0x00ea2596` is not a second
  Lua stack accessor at all, it is the compiler's own inlined float64-to-int64 rounding cast, called
  immediately after and operating only on the x87 register `lua_tonumber` left behind. [CONFIRMED —
  disassembly, §4.1.]**

Every function below returns via the real `lua_CFunction` convention: a literal `return 0;` (or a
decompiler-inferred `void` fall-through with no `lua_push*` call in the body, which is the same
thing — zero Lua values pushed) means no Lua return value; a literal `return 1;` preceded by a
`0x00dfe590` push means exactly one Lua return value.

## 1. Trigger/mission/objective cluster — 12 functions, all in the 1,014-entry gameplay table (`0x00a20840`)

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was the 12 highest real-script-call-count names from
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.4's cross-team join (`trigger_enable` 563 calls/59 scripts down to
`object_is_in_trigger` 86/19) that were not already covered by another concurrent pass on this same
new document. All 12 were confirmed present in the 1,014-entry gameplay array exactly as expected;
none needed to fall back to the UI (`0x008430f0`) or third (`0x00845aa0`) registrar. Each entry's
paired function pointer was recovered by taking the full ordered list of every
`MOV dword ptr [stack],imm32` instruction inside `0x00a20840`'s body (`0x00a20840`–`0x00a25f7e`,
2,028 such instructions total, matching 1,014 name/1,014 function pairs with no other instruction
shape competing for the count) and reading the entry immediately following each target name's own
slot — i.e., the same `{namePtr,funcPtr}` adjacency this document's method section and
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.1/§13.2 already established structurally. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly;
full ordered list read directly, not sampled; raw evidence preserved at
`tools/lua_gp_target_pairs.txt`, which also prints ±2/±3 neighbouring array entries around every
target for manual cross-check — every neighbour resolves cleanly to a real name or a real code
address, confirming no misalignment.]** None of the 12 function-pointer targets had previously been
marked as a Ghidra function-start in this project's database (the same "valid code, not yet
boundary-fixed" situation already documented for roughly half of the third registrar's targets,
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.5) — each was force-disassembled and given a function boundary as part of
this pass before decompiling.

### 1.1 `trigger_enable` (`0x00a617d0`) — 563 calls / 59 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory + 2 optional. Arg 1 (string, mandatory) — a trigger name. Arg 2
(boolean, optional, default `true`) — enable/disable. Arg 3 (numeric/flag value, optional, default
`3`) — read via the ~~unresolved flag-extractor pair~~ `lua_tonumber` + integer conversion pair (`0x00dfe160`/`0x00ea2596`, resolved §4.1)
and later tested against bit `0x2`.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`, no push).

**Body:** the trigger name (arg 1) is resolved to a handle via a shared by-name resolver
(`0x005e4e30`) also used by three other functions in this cluster (§1.2/§1.7/§1.12), then gated by
a shared handle-liveness check (`0x00853b10`, returns non-zero for a dead/invalid handle — used
identically by every named-object resolution in this cluster). If the handle is alive: when bit
`0x2` of the arg-3 flag value is set, a setter (`0x0093dbc0`) is called with the handle and the
enable boolean; then, depending on the enable boolean, one of two further subsystem calls
(`0x0093d320` for enable, `0x0093bde0` for disable) is made, each apparently taking only the flag
value in the visible decompilation — **[OPEN — the decompiler shows only 1 explicit argument at
these two tail calls; a hidden calling-convention argument (e.g. the handle passed via a register)
is likely, but not resolved here — does not change the Lua-visible signature above.]**

**Side effects / subsystem:** mutates trigger-subsystem state for the named trigger (an
enable/disable toggle plus a flag-gated secondary behaviour switch). Subsystem: mission/trigger
state. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for control flow and argument shape; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the
exact role of the flag bit and the two tail setters, whose own internal semantics were not traced
further.]**

### 1.2 `on_trigger` (`0x00a58680`) — 513 calls / 59 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, no optional trailing arguments. Arg 1 — kept as an opaque
string (never resolved through a name lookup itself), used only as a value handed to a
registration call — consistent with a callback/handler name. Arg 2 — a trigger name, resolved via
the same shared resolver as §1.1 (`0x005e4e30`) and gated by the same liveness check
(`0x00853b10`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** once the trigger handle (arg 2) is resolved and alive, a per-trigger field at handle
offset `+0xa8` is checked; if it reads as unset (`0`), a local mode value of `0` together with arg 1
(the callback name) is passed into a registration function (`0x00a56cb0`) — this is the same
registration function §1.7 (`on_trigger_exit`) calls with mode value `1`, strongly suggesting
`+0xa8` is a single callback-list slot on the trigger object tagged by an enter(`0`)/exit(`1`) mode,
not two separate fields. A second field at handle offset `+0xf8` is then checked (`!= -1`); if so,
`0x00d9e140(0)` is called. **Correction, 2026-09-30 (a later pass's direct decompilation of
`0x00d9e140` itself, while documenting an unrelated function that also calls it): this is NOT a
flush/notify call, as this section originally characterized it.** Its real body adds its integer
argument to a fixed global base value and wraps the sum into a fixed range (via a constant-offset
correction of 1,800,000,000), then writes the result through a hidden pointer argument — a
deadline/timestamp computation ("now plus N units, wrapped into a fixed cycle"), not a queue,
broadcast, or opcode-tagged record of any kind. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, `0x00d9e140`'s own
body.]** What this specific call site (argument literal `0`, i.e. "now, no offset") actually does
with the computed timestamp is not established here — the hidden pointer's destination for THIS
call site was not traced — so the reading of `+0xf8`'s check as "pending enter-callback state" is
retained as a plausible motivation for computing a timestamp at all, but "flush/notify" specifically
is withdrawn as a mischaracterization of the callee, not merely refined.

**Side effects / subsystem:** registers a Lua-callable callback name against the named trigger's
enter-mode callback slot. Subsystem: mission/trigger-state (callback registration).
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for control flow, field offsets, and the shared registration-function
identity with §1.7; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the semantic reading of the mode tag / `+0xf8` ~~flush~~ pending-state check (callee computes a timestamp, see correction above).]**

### 1.3 `objective_text` (`0x00a56920`) — 424 calls / 41 scripts

**Arguments:** 6 total. Arg 1 (numeric/slot value, mandatory, read via the same ~~unresolved~~
flag/number-extractor pair as §1.1's arg 3 — `lua_tonumber` + integer conversion, resolved §4.1) — an objective-slot index. Arg 2 (string, mandatory) —
a text key. Arg 3 (string, optional, default a shared empty-string constant). Arg 4 (string,
optional, default the same shared empty-string constant). Arg 5 (numeric/flag, optional, default
`3`, same extractor pair). Arg 6 (numeric/flag, optional, default `0`, same extractor pair).

**Return:** none — no `lua_push*`-shaped call appears anywhere in the body (decompiler infers
`void`), consistent with 0 Lua return values.

**Body:** arg 2 (the text key) is passed to a localization-key resolver (`0x00849df0`); if that
fails, and a global gate (a single flag checked with no further identification attempted here) is
set, a second resolver pair (`0x00604740`→`0x00604500`) is tried; if that also fails, the raw key
string itself is formatted into a 512-byte local buffer via what reads as a `sprintf`-shaped
formatter (`0x00db06e0`) as a last-resort literal fallback. Whatever text pointer results, together
with the slot index (arg 1), the two optional strings (args 3/4), and the two optional flag values
(args 5/6), is handed to one final call, `0x007ee110` — six parameters, matching the task brief's
own prediction of "a global objective-text UI slot."

**Side effects / subsystem:** writes a resolved (localized, or raw-fallback) objective string, plus
two auxiliary strings and two flag values, into a global objective-text/HUD slot identified by the
slot index. Subsystem: mission/objective UI (HUD text). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full
argument chain and call graph; HIGH CONFIDENCE that `0x007ee110` is the actual UI-slot writer, since
its address sits immediately adjacent to §1.4's clearing counterpart (`0x007eda00`) and takes
exactly the shape the source arguments assemble; the localization-fallback global gate's exact
meaning is OPEN.]**

### 1.4 `objective_text_clear` (`0x00a56ab0`) — 263 calls / 45 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory numeric value (an objective-slot index), read unconditionally via the
same flag/number-extractor pair used for §1.3's arg 1 and arg 3/5/6 — no optionality check at all,
so this argument is always read as if present.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** after reading the slot index, a zero-argument helper (`0x00d1e0c0`) is called (read as a
housekeeping/refresh step), then the slot index itself is passed to `0x007eda00` — the direct
counterpart to §1.3's `0x007ee110` (same subsystem region, opposite "set"/"clear" role).

**Side effects / subsystem:** clears the named objective-text/HUD slot. Subsystem: mission/objective
UI (HUD text). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for control flow and argument shape; HIGH CONFIDENCE for
the "clear" role assignment, inferred from address proximity and shape symmetry with §1.3 rather
than independently decompiled further.]**

### 1.5 `mission_end_failure` (`0x00a523e0`) — 160 calls / 36 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings. Arg 1 — passed as-is (never handle-resolved) into a gate
function (`0x006d7240`) that returns a pass/fail boolean; the whole function is a no-op if this gate
fails. Arg 2 — a failure-reason/localization key.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`, on both the gated-out path and the normal path).

**Body:** once the arg-1 gate passes, arg 2 is resolved to an internal id via `0x00604740`, then to
a wide (localized) string via `0x00604500`; a cleanup/bookkeeping call (`0x006d00e0`) runs on arg 2
regardless. If no localized string was found: a literal `"NULL"` wide string is used if arg 2 was
itself empty/zero, otherwise a second, different localization-key resolver (`0x00849df0` — the same
one §1.3 uses) is tried, falling back to a literal `"FAILURE STRING NOT LOCALIZED"` wide string if
that also fails. Whatever wide string results is handed, together with two shared global default
parameters (repeated twice in the call), to a final dispatch (`0x006da400`).

**Side effects / subsystem:** displays a mission-failure message (resolved localized text, or a
diagnostic fallback string) via a UI/dialog subsystem, gated on an arg-1 mission-state check.
Subsystem: mission state + UI dialog/HUD text. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full resolver
chain and gating; HIGH CONFIDENCE for "arg 1 identifies the mission being checked/failed" — the
gate function `0x006d7240` itself was not separately decompiled.]**

### 1.6 `mission_set_checkpoint` (`0x00a52600`) — 157 calls / 37 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (a checkpoint/mission name) + 2 optional booleans, each defaulting
to `false` when absent or nil, read via the same nil-test-then-`lua_toboolean` idiom as §1.1's arg 2.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the three values (name string, both booleans) are passed directly to one call,
`0x006d5060` — no name-resolver/handle-lookup step at all in this function, unlike every other
function in this cluster that takes a name argument.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets a checkpoint identified by name, modified by two boolean flags
whose individual meaning was not traced past this call. Subsystem: mission/checkpoint state.
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument shape and the single dispatch call; OPEN — the two boolean
flags' individual semantics, and why this entry point skips the handle-resolution step every sibling
function uses.]**

### 1.7 `on_trigger_exit` (`0x00a58720`) — 104 calls / 23 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, identical shape to §1.2 (`on_trigger`): arg 1 an opaque
callback-name string, arg 2 a trigger name resolved via the same shared resolver (`0x005e4e30`) and
liveness check (`0x00853b10`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** structurally identical to §1.2 except for two literal differences: the mode value passed
into the shared registration function (`0x00a56cb0`) is `1` instead of `0` (exit vs. enter — see
§1.2's reading of trigger-object offset `+0xa8` as one mode-tagged callback slot), and the
"already-pending" field checked afterward is at handle offset `+0xfc` rather than §1.2's `+0xf8` —
i.e. a second, adjacent per-trigger pending-~~flush~~state dword dedicated to the exit path ("flush" withdrawn, see §1.2's correction).

**Side effects / subsystem:** registers a Lua-callable callback name against the named trigger's
exit-mode callback slot. Subsystem: mission/trigger-state (callback registration). **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly, direct structural comparison against §1.2's own confirmed reading.]**

### 1.8 `spawn_region_enable` (`0x00a5fc00`) — 104 calls / 14 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory, both read unconditionally with no absence/nil check: arg 1 (string) a
spawn-region name, arg 2 (boolean) an enable flag.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 is resolved via a resolver distinct from every other function in this cluster
(`0x006ed4d0` — a spawn-region-specific registry, not the trigger/object resolver `0x005e4e30`
§1.1/§1.2/§1.7/§1.12 share), gated by the same shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`). If alive, a
single bit (bit `0`) of a byte field at handle offset `+0x94` is set to the arg-2 boolean value via
a branchless conditional-XOR idiom, leaving the field's other 7 bits untouched.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets or clears bit `0x1` of a per-spawn-region byte flag at handle
`+0x94`. Subsystem: ambient/spawn-region state. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, including the exact
single-bit-only scope of the write, verified from the bitwise expression itself.]**

### 1.9 `city_zone_swap` (`0x00a43460`) — 104 calls / 22 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (a city-zone/pair name) + 1 optional boolean (default `true` when
absent or nil).

**Return:** none — no `lua_push*` call in the body (decompiler infers `void`), consistent with 0
Lua return values.

**Body:** unconditionally, before anything else, a bookkeeping call (`0x00d9e8b0`) is made with the
zone name and two literal arguments (`0` and `-1`), read as clearing/priming any pending swap state
keyed by that name. Then a debug/dev-mode double gate (two zero-argument checks, `0x006cecb0` and
`0x006cec60`) is evaluated; **if and only if both are true**, the *current* zone name (fetched via a
third zero-argument getter, `0x006cfeb0`) is compared against the arg-1 string (via a fixed-size
local-buffer copy plus a direct `strncmp`-shaped comparison against a value read through
`0x00e0ceb0`); on a match, a different, immediate-apply entry point (`0x006cfdb0`) is called with
the name and the boolean, and the function returns early — a dev/debug-only short-circuit path. In
every other case (debug gate false, or names don't match), one of two normal-path subsystem entries
is called depending on the boolean: `0x0084a940` if `false`, `0x0084a910` if `true`.

**Side effects / subsystem:** queues (or, only under an active debug/dev configuration when the
target zone matches the currently-loaded zone, immediately applies) a city-zone swap keyed by name.
Subsystem: world/zone-streaming. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure and call
graph; HIGH CONFIDENCE that the two zero-argument gates are a debug/dev-mode check specifically —
inferred from their use as a short-circuit around the normal deferred-swap path, not independently
decompiled.]**

### 1.10 `door_open` (`0x00a488c0`) — 101 calls / 21 scripts

**Arguments:** 6 total — the richest signature in this cluster. Arg 1 (string, mandatory) — a door
name. Arg 2 (boolean, optional, default `false`). Arg 3 (boolean, optional, default `true`). Arg 4
(string, optional, default absent/`0`). Arg 5 (string, optional, default absent/`0`). Arg 6 (string,
optional, default absent/`0`) — each of args 2–6 individually guarded by the same nil-test idiom
used throughout this cluster, decremented one remaining-argument slot at a time.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (boolean-shaped) — a real `0x00dfe590` push followed by a literal
`return 1;`.

**Body:** arg 1 resolves to a door handle via yet another distinct by-name resolver
(`0x006434a0`), gated by the shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`). If arg 4 is absent, a simple
open call (`0x00a31920`) is made with just the two booleans (args 2/3) and its result becomes the
pushed return value. If arg 4 IS present, it is itself resolved via a second by-name resolver
(`0x00a281a0`) to a secondary handle; if that succeeds and a field at door-handle offset `+200` (0xc8)
is non-zero (read as "this door has an attached lock/mechanism"), arg 5 is resolved via
`0x004bf810` and applied via `0x00944f90`; if arg 6 is also present, it resolves via a third by-name
resolver (`0x005982e0`) to a tertiary handle, gated by the same liveness check again, and — if
alive — a formatted buffer is built (`0x004b74f0`) and dispatched through an indirect call read off
the secondary handle's own function-pointer table at offset `+0x48` (a virtual/callback dispatch,
not a fixed engine function). Success is signalled by pushing `1`; any failed branch pushes `0`.

**Side effects / subsystem:** opens the named door; when the richer optional arguments are supplied,
also interacts with a second named object (read as a lock/mechanism) and, transitively, a third
named object via a callback dispatch. Subsystem: world/interactive-object (door) state.
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure, argument shape, and resolver chain;
OPEN — the exact real-world meaning of door-handle field `+0xc8`, and the identity of whatever class
owns the secondary handle's `+0x48` vtable-shaped slot, were not traced further.]**

### 1.11 `on_dismiss` (`0x00a57dd0`) — 100 calls / 25 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, the same surface shape as §1.2/§1.7 (`on_trigger`/
`on_trigger_exit`): arg 1 an opaque callback-name string, arg 2 a name resolved through a by-name
lookup and the shared liveness check.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** structurally the same registration pattern as §1.2/§1.7, but with two differences that
together point at a genuinely different object category: arg 2 is resolved through a *different*
by-name resolver, `0x005e4dd0` (not the trigger/object resolver `0x005e4e30` §1.1/§1.2/§1.7/§1.12
share), and the callback is registered via a *different* setter, `0x005e4660`, with a literal mode
value of `10` (not `0`/`1` as in §1.2/§1.7). There is no second "pending-~~flush~~state" field check
afterward, unlike §1.2/§1.7.

**Side effects / subsystem:** registers a Lua-callable callback name against a named object of a
different kind than the trigger objects §1.2/§1.7 target (mode-slot `10`) — the name "on_dismiss"
and the distinct resolver together read most plausibly as a companion/NPC ("homie") dismissal
callback rather than a trigger one, though the resolved object's exact class was not independently
confirmed. Subsystem: AI/companion object callback-registration (or, more generally, a second
named-object registry distinct from the trigger one). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the structural
differences from §1.2/§1.7; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the callback-registration role; OPEN — the resolved
object's exact class/subsystem identity.]** **[Resolved by §3: `0x005e4dd0` is the character resolver (§3 preamble) and `0x005e4660` the character hook-slot-array writer (§3.3); `on_dismiss` registers character hook slot `10` (character-kind attribution per §3's preamble label).]**

### 1.12 `object_is_in_trigger` (`0x00a57720`) — 86 calls / 19 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, both read unconditionally: arg 1 an object name, arg 2 a
trigger name.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (boolean-shaped) — a real `0x00dfe590` push followed by a literal
`return 1;`.

**Body:** arg 1 resolves to a handle via the same shared resolver as §1.1/§1.2/§1.7
(`0x005e4e30`), gated by the shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`); if either step fails, a local
"object resolved" flag is left at `0`, but the function still unconditionally proceeds to parse arg
2 (the trigger name) via a separate helper (`0x00a455a0`) into two local output records (12 and 36
bytes) — read as decomposing a trigger reference into its underlying geometric/positional
representation, exact field meanings **[OPEN]** (cf. §4.2: `0x00a455a0` is the shared name→world-position lookup, so the 12-byte record is plausibly the resolved position — not independently confirmed). Only if BOTH the arg-1 object resolved successfully
AND the arg-2 parse succeeded is an actual containment test performed, via `0x0093bfc0` against the
first (12-byte) parsed record; the pushed result is that test's boolean, or `0` if either
precondition failed.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none (a pure query; no state-mutating call was found in the body).
Answers "is the named object currently inside the named trigger volume." Subsystem: mission/trigger
state (read-only query). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full gating logic and call graph;
OPEN — the exact contents of the two records `0x00a455a0` produces, and why the containment test
`0x0093bfc0` is passed only the first record with no other argument visible in the decompilation
(a hidden calling-convention argument, e.g. the resolved object handle carried in a register, is
the likely explanation but was not independently confirmed).]**

### 1.13 Cross-function observations

Four distinct by-name resolver/registry pairs were found across these 12 functions, each paired
with the same shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`) regardless of which resolver produced the
handle — good evidence `0x00853b10` is a generic, object-kind-agnostic handle-validity guard, not
something specific to triggers: trigger/generic-object (`0x005e4e30`, used by §1.1/§1.2/§1.7/§1.12),
spawn-region (`0x006ed4d0`, §1.8), door (`0x006434a0`, §1.10), and a fourth, non-trigger resolver
(`0x005e4dd0`, §1.11) whose target object category is the one open question in this set (**[Resolved: character resolver, §3 preamble/§3.3.]**). Two
independent "set slot"/"clear slot" pairs were also confirmed by address adjacency and argument-shape
symmetry alone, without needing to decompile the setter's own body further:
`objective_text`/`objective_text_clear` (`0x007ee110`/`0x007eda00`, §1.3/§1.4) and the enter/exit
callback-mode pair sharing one registration function (`0x00a56cb0`, §1.2/§1.7). No function in this
cluster touches a global objective-text UI slot AND a trigger-state table at the same time — the
task brief's guess that this cluster "plausibly touches a mission/trigger-state table, a global
objective-text UI slot, or similar" resolves cleanly into two disjoint families: trigger/object
state (§1.1/§1.2/§1.7/§1.8/§1.9/§1.10/§1.11/§1.12) and objective/HUD-text state (§1.3/§1.4), plus two
outliers that touch neither directly — mission-checkpoint/failure dispatch calls
(§1.5/§1.6) whose own internal state representation was not traced past the single dispatch
function each one calls.

**Recommendation for a future pass (not attempted here, out of this task's static-only scope):** a
behavioural oracle (real input/output vectors from actually running e.g. `door_open` with its
richer optional-argument combinations, or `trigger_enable`'s flag-bit-`0x2` branch) would settle
several of this section's OPEN items — the door-handle `+0xc8` field's real meaning, the two
`mission_set_checkpoint` booleans, and `object_is_in_trigger`'s apparent hidden argument — far
faster than further static tracing. This is a recommendation only; building or running such an
oracle is explicitly out of scope for this task.

## 2. Platform/audio/input/UI-utility cluster — 10 functions, ranked by real script-call count (peer census)

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was the 10 functions the task brief supplied directly from
a peer team's own script-census cross-reference against `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13's full registered
roster: `game_get_platform` (659 calls/244 scripts), `game_UI_audio_play` (616/158), `game_get_key_name`
(442/76), `audio_object_post_event` (427/47), `audio_play_persona_line` (227/36),
`game_is_active_input_gamepad` (238/147), `game_peg_unload` (122/41), `pop_screen` (106/45), `fade_out`
(94/53), `audio_conversation_play` (129/41). Six names (`game_get_platform`, `game_UI_audio_play`,
`audio_object_post_event`, `audio_play_persona_line`, `game_peg_unload`, `audio_conversation_play`) were
found exactly once each, as predicted, inside the 1,014-entry gameplay registrar (`0x00a20840`); three
(`game_get_key_name`, `pop_screen`) plus `game_UI_audio_play`'s own duplicate-name-string slot were found
inside the 113-entry loop registrar (`0x00845aa0`) already fully walked by `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.5.
`game_is_active_input_gamepad` was checked against both, per the task brief's own steer — it is a real,
literal dual registration (§2.11).

Every `{namePtr,funcPtr}` pair used below was read directly from this document's and
`spec-lua-bindings.md`'s own already-published raw array walks — no new name search was needed:
`0x00845aa0`'s 113 pairs from `tools/lua_game845aa0_full.txt` (already public, §13.5), and
`0x00a20840`'s 1,014 pairs from a companion full ordered-pair walk of the same function
(`tools/scratchpad/lua_gameplay_1014_raw_pairs.txt`, same method as `tools/lua_gp_target_pairs.txt` in
§1: every `MOV dword ptr [stack],imm32` in the function body, in address order, each name-string entry
paired with its immediate successor). Five of the ten target addresses had not yet been marked as a
Ghidra function start (`0x843fa0`, `0xa3d050`, `0x845650`, `0x842aa0`, `0xa49dc0` — the same "valid
code, not yet boundary-fixed" situation `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.5 and this document's §1 both
already record for roughly half of their own targets); each was force-disassembled and given a function
boundary before decompiling. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, all ten pairs read directly from the two raw
walks, not sampled.]**

**Primitive identification for this cluster — independently re-derived, upgrading this document's own
§1 from HIGH CONFIDENCE to CONFIRMED for five shared primitives.** Every one of these ten functions
opens with the identical machine-generated `lua_CFunction` prologue §1's method section already
describes (a `lua_gettop` call, then positional/optional argument extraction). This pass went one level
deeper than §1's argument-shape matching: it independently decompiled the *primitives' own bodies* (not
just their call-site argument counts) and matched each one structurally, line-for-line, against real
published Lua 5.1 interpreter source (`lapi.c`/`lauxlib.c`/`lobject.c`/`lstring.c`/`lvm.c` — Lua is
MIT-licensed and its own source is public, the same citation basis `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.1 already
used for `lua_pushcclosure`/`lua_setfield`/`luaI_openlib`):

- **`0x00dfde50(L)`** — body is exactly `(L->top − L->base) >> 4` (a byte-address subtraction shifted
  by 4, i.e. divided by 16 — this project's own already-established `TValue` size). This is the real
  public **`lua_gettop`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE
  reading of the same address.]**
- **`0x00dfdc60(L, idx)`** — the shared internal stack-index-to-pointer helper every other primitive
  below calls first; matches the real Lua 5.1 internal `index2adr`. Not itself public API, cited only
  as supporting evidence. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, structural match.]**
- **`0x00dfe040(L, idx)`** — calls `index2adr`, returns `-1` (`LUA_TNONE`) if the result is the
  interpreter's shared nil-sentinel object, else returns the resolved value's type tag. This is the
  real public **`lua_type`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE
  reading of the same address.]** Lua 5.1's own tag constants (`LUA_TNIL`=0, `LUA_TBOOLEAN`=1,
  `LUA_TNUMBER`=3, `LUA_TSTRING`=4, `LUA_TTABLE`=5) resolve every `==`/`!=` comparison against this
  call's result seen below.
- **`0x00dfe160(L, idx)`** — calls `index2adr`; if the tag isn't `LUA_TNUMBER`, calls an internal
  numeric-coercion helper (structurally `luaV_tonumber`) and bails to `0` on failure; otherwise returns
  the value's number field directly, in the real x87 floating-point return register — the real public
  **`lua_tonumber`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly. This resolves §1's own explicitly OPEN
  item about this same address: it is `lua_tonumber`, not an unidentified "flags/number extractor."]**
- **`0x00ea2596()`** — a zero-`lua_State`-argument float64-to-int64 rounding routine matching the
  classic compiler-generated (MSVC) round-half-correcting float-to-integer conversion helper (exact rounding semantics OPEN, see §4.1), always
  seen immediately after a `0x00dfe160` (`lua_tonumber`) call still holding its result in the FPU
  register. This is **not** a distinct Lua API entry point — it is the compiler's own emitted cast code
  for a source-level `(int)lua_tonumber(L, idx)` expression (or the real public `lua_tointeger`, which
  is defined in terms of exactly this same coercion-then-truncate sequence and is observably
  indistinguishable from it at this call shape). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the pairing and role;
  HIGH CONFIDENCE for treating it as equivalent to `lua_tointeger` rather than a hand-written cast, the
  two not being distinguishable from machine code alone.]**
- **`0x00dfe210(L, idx, 0)`** — calls `index2adr`; if not already a string, calls the internal
  `luaV_tostring` coercion, then (matching the real source's own comment that "the previous call may
  reallocate the stack") re-resolves the index via `index2adr` a second time before reading the
  string's length/data fields. This is the real public **`lua_tolstring`**/**`lua_tostring`** (the
  latter being `lua_tolstring(L,idx,NULL)`) line-for-line, including the exact stack-reallocation
  re-fetch its own real source is known for. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE
  reading of the same address.]**
- **`0x00dfe1e0(L, idx)`** — calls `index2adr`, returns `0` only for the nil tag or for the boolean tag
  with a zero value, `1` otherwise — the real public **`lua_toboolean`** line-for-line (`!l_isfalse`).
  **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE reading of the same address.]**
- **`0x00dfe3a0(L, n)`** — writes `n` into the slot at `L->top`, sets its tag to `LUA_TNUMBER`,
  advances `top`. Real public **`lua_pushnumber`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe420(L, s)`** — if `s` is `NULL`, writes a `LUA_TNIL`-tagged slot directly (the real
  `lua_pushnil` fast path `lua_pushstring` takes for a `NULL` argument); otherwise, BEFORE interning,
  calls a GC-threshold check (structurally `luaC_checkGC`, also called standalone elsewhere as
  `0x00e014b0`) — this call site's own instruction order places it ahead of the interning step, matching
  where real `lua_pushlstring` calls `luaC_checkGC` (a totalbytes-vs-threshold compare), not the separate
  internal string-table load-factor/resize check that real Lua only runs on a cache-miss inside interning
  itself (not independently re-derived which exact fields `0x00e014b0` compares, only that its call
  position matches the GC-check site, not the resize site) — then interns the string via an internal
  helper (structurally `luaS_newlstr`), and pushes it tagged `LUA_TSTRING`. Real public
  **`lua_pushstring`** line-for-line
  (`lua_pushnil` + `lua_pushlstring` inlined together, matching the real source's own
  `if (s==NULL) lua_pushnil(L); else lua_pushlstring(L,s,strlen(s));` body). **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe590(L, b)`** — writes a `LUA_TBOOLEAN`-tagged slot with value `(b != 0)`, advances `top`.
  Real public **`lua_pushboolean`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH
  CONFIDENCE reading of the same address, and resolves the "not independently distinguished from
  `lua_pushinteger`" caveat §1 flagged — the tag written is unambiguously `LUA_TBOOLEAN`.]**
- **`0x00dfde60(L, idx)`** — for a negative `idx`, adjusts `top` by `(idx+1)*16` bytes; for a
  non-negative `idx`, nil-fills up to `base+idx*16` then sets `top` there. Real public **`lua_settop`**
  line-for-line, including both the positive- and negative-index branches. **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly.]** Every observed call site in this cluster uses it with a small negative literal (e.g.
  `-2`) purely to pop values off the stack after a `lua_gettable`-style read.
- **`0x00dfe5e0(L, idx)`** — resolves `idx` via `index2adr`, then calls an internal helper
  (structurally `luaV_gettable`) with the resolved table and `L->top-1` as both key and destination —
  the real public **`lua_gettable`** line-for-line (an in-place pop-key/push-value). **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe380`/`0x00dfec70`** — seen only inside `audio_object_post_event`'s table-length helper
  (§2.4), in the exact compiled shape of a `for k,v in pairs(t) do … end` loop counting entries (push,
  advance-or-stop, pop, repeat). Consistent with the real public **`lua_pushnil`**/**`lua_next`** pair
  respectively, but their own bodies were not independently opened this pass. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE —
  inferred from calling-pattern shape only, not opened directly; unlike the primitives above, not
  upgraded to CONFIRMED.]**
- **`AK::SoundEngine::GetIDFromString`** — a real, publicly-documented Audiokinetic Wwise SDK symbol,
  recovered directly from the binary's own linked-symbol table (not a guess), reached from a shared
  name-resolver two of this cluster's functions call (`0x00462960`→`0x0046fd00`, §2.2/§2.4/§2.5). The
  wrapper treats the literal string `"none"` (case-insensitively) and an empty string as sentinels for
  "no sound"/"invalid" and skips the real Wwise call entirely in that case. **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly; the symbol name itself is read directly off the binary's own import/name table, not
  inferred — consistent with this project's already-published "Audio: Wwise + wrapper" finding,
  `spec-audio-format.md`.]**
- **`GetKeyNameTextW`** — the real public Win32 API, called from an internal key/button-name helper
  (`0x005be0d0`, §2.3) reached from `game_get_key_name`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; symbol recovered
  directly.]**

### 2.1 `game_get_platform` (`0x00841c50`) — 659 calls / 244 scripts

**Arguments:** none used. `lua_gettop` is still called first (the shared prologue, §2's method note)
but its result is never read again anywhere in the body — every argument passed by a caller is
silently ignored.

**Return:** 1 Lua value — a `lua_pushstring` call followed by `return 1;`.

**Body:** pushes one fixed, compile-time literal string, `"PC"` (read directly from `.rdata` at the
pushed address), and returns it. No branching, no other engine state read or written.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none — a pure, constant-returning query. Subsystem: platform/build
identification. Consistent with the already-documented `game_is_pc_dx11`/`game_get_ps3_button_swap`
sibling names in the same registrar (`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.4) — this build's answer is
unconditionally `"PC"`, with no runtime platform-detection logic at all. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly,
full body read; the literal string content was read directly from `.rdata`, not inferred from the
function's name.]**

### 2.2 `game_UI_audio_play` (`0x008439e0`) — 616 calls / 158 scripts

**Arguments:** 1, optional. If `lua_gettop` reports at least one argument, argument 1 is read
polymorphically: `lua_type` first; if `LUA_TSTRING`, the string is read via `lua_tolstring` and passed
through the Wwise name-resolver (`0x00462960`→`AK::SoundEngine::GetIDFromString`, §2's method note);
otherwise it is read as a number via `lua_tonumber` and truncated to an integer directly (treated as an
already-resolved sound ID). If zero arguments are passed, this resolution step is skipped entirely and
the resolved-sound-id local stays `0`.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a number) — `lua_pushnumber` then `return 1;`.

**Body:** independently of whether argument 1 resolved to anything, a fixed literal category name,
`"UI"`, is also resolved through the same Wwise-ID resolver. A voice/emitter object is then created via
a heavily stack-protected helper (`0x0045da50`) called with a null position pointer, the `"UI"`
category-id argument, and a literal flag `1` — read as "create a non-positional (2D) voice tagged to
the UI audio category." If both the sound-id and category resolved successfully, a binder call
(`0x0045f5b0`) associates the resolved sound with the new voice; a start/commit call (`0x0045ea70`)
follows unconditionally, its output out-parameter becoming the value eventually pushed back to Lua; a
final flag-setting call (`0x0045e170`) sets one bit on the voice object (bit `0x4000` at the voice's own
`+0x98` field — a "release after play"/auto-cleanup marker, the same field and companion bit `0x20`
`0x0045f5b0` itself sets during binding).

**Side effects / subsystem:** creates a 2D (non-positional) Wwise voice/emitter tagged to a fixed
`"UI"` audio category, optionally binds a caller-supplied sound (by name or by already-resolved
numeric id) to it, starts playback, and marks the voice for automatic release once finished. Returns
the resulting voice/play-instance handle as a Lua number, or a handle to an unbound, still-created
voice if no sound argument was given. Subsystem: audio (Wwise-backed 2D UI sound-effect playback — a
distinct, lighter-weight path from the full event/switch-value machinery `audio_object_post_event`
uses, §2.4). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument reading, resolver calls, and the overall
create→bind→start→flag call sequence; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the exact role of the two flag bits set on
the voice object's `+0x98` field, whose owning class was not independently identified.]**

### 2.3 `game_get_key_name` (`0x00843fa0`) — 442 calls / 76 scripts

**Arguments:** 1, read unconditionally (no absence/nil check — `lua_gettop`'s result is used directly
to compute the argument's stack index with no presence test first, unlike every other function in this
cluster). Read via `lua_tonumber` then truncated to an integer — a numeric key/button code.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a string) — `lua_pushstring` then implicit `return` (the decompiler shows no
explicit trailing `return 1;` statement, but the call shape — one `lua_pushstring` and nothing else
pushed — is the same one-return-value contract as every other single-push function in this document).

**Body:** the integer code is passed to a small forwarder (`0x005be2a0`) which reaches a key-name
lookup helper (`0x005be0d0`). That helper's own body handles three distinct input shapes: the literal
sentinel `0xffffffff` (integer `-1`) resolves to a localization tag, `"PC_UNBOUND_KEY"`; small values
`0`–`6` index a fixed table of localization tags for the seven mouse buttons (a separate table variant
selected by a caller-supplied byte flag not independently traced from this call site); any other value
in that same low range falls back to a literal `"MENU_INVALID_MOUSE"` tag; values outside that whole
range are passed to the real public Win32 `GetKeyNameTextW`, then re-encoded. **[OPEN — this call
site's own argument marshalling into `0x005be0d0` shows a visible mismatch between the three arguments
the call site passes and the three-plus-hidden-register arguments the callee's own recovered signature
uses, so which of these branches this specific call site actually reaches was not pinned down with
full confidence; does not affect the confirmed overall input/output contract below.]** Whatever
localized tag or raw key name results, if it came from `GetKeyNameTextW`, is walked through a
second helper (`0x00e22a30`) that re-encodes a UTF-16 string into this project's own escaped
byte-stream text format (a header byte `0x80` then one three-byte record per character, using escape
markers `0x01`/`0x03`/`0x04` for special cases, terminated `0x08`) before being pushed.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none beyond local buffers — a pure query. Resolves a numeric
key/mouse-button code to its localized, display-ready name string. Subsystem: input (key/button
naming) plus this project's own text/localization encoding layer. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the
overall call chain, the `GetKeyNameTextW` call, and the re-encoding step; OPEN for the exact branch
selected at this specific call site, per above.]**

### 2.4 `audio_object_post_event` (`0x00a3cb00`) — 427 calls / 47 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory, up to 4 further optional (richest signature in this cluster).

- **Arg 1 (string, mandatory):** an event name, read via `lua_tolstring` and resolved through the same
  Wwise-ID resolver `0x00462960`/`AK::SoundEngine::GetIDFromString` used in §2.2/§2.5. If resolution
  fails, the function pushes `lua_pushnumber(0)` and returns immediately (1 Lua value, value `0`).
- **Arg 2 (optional):** read polymorphically by `lua_type`. If `LUA_TSTRING`, one value is resolved
  through the same name-resolver. If `LUA_TTABLE`, the table is walked via a dedicated length-then-loop
  helper (`0x0083dff0`, detailed below) collecting up to 2 resolved values — a table reporting *more*
  than 2 elements aborts the whole function immediately with the same `push 0; return 1;` failure path
  used for a failed arg-1 resolution.
- **Arg 3 (optional):** identical shape to arg 2 (string-or-table-of-≤2), a second independent
  value/list.
- **Arg 4 (string, optional):** a game-object name. The literal `"#PLAYER1_VEHICLE#"` is special-cased
  (case-insensitively, via the real public CRT `_stricmp`) to redirect to whatever object the separate
  literal `"#PLAYER1#"` resolves to; any other name is resolved through a distinct object-by-name
  lookup (`0x00a29200`). Either way, a resulting object's stored position pair is read (via
  `0x004dcc60`, which itself reads one of two alternate position-field pairs on the object depending on
  a liveness/validity check of the first pair); if arg 4 is absent or fails to resolve, a global
  fallback position pair (`0x0117f808`/`0x0117f80c`) is used instead.
- **Arg 5 (boolean, optional):** read via `lua_toboolean`; **defaults to `true`** if absent or nil —
  the only argument in this whole ten-function cluster observed defaulting a boolean to `true` when
  the corresponding presence-check helper (`lua_type`) reports the slot doesn't exist, rather than when
  it reports the value present-but-nil (both paths reach the same `true` default here).

**Table-walk helper (`0x0083dff0`), used for arg 2/arg 3:** first attempts to read the table's own
`n` field (the classic pre-`#`-operator Lua length convention: pushes the literal string `"n"`, calls
`lua_gettable`) and, if that is a number, uses it directly as the count. Only if `t.n` is absent or not
a number does it fall back to a real generic table walk in the exact compiled shape of
`for k,v in pairs(t) do count = count + 1 end` (§2's method note, `0x00dfe380`/`0x00dfec70`) to count
real entries. Either way, it then re-walks indices `1..count` via `lua_gettable`, resolving each
element through the shared Wwise-ID resolver.

**Return:** normally 1 Lua value (a number: the resulting post-event/play-instance handle, or `0` on
any resolution failure). **Exceptionally 2 values** — a leading `lua_pushnumber(0)` followed by the
normal handle push — specifically when arg 2's and arg 3's resolved-list *counts* differ from each
other; the function does not treat this mismatch as a hard failure, it just prepends an extra `0`
before continuing normally.

**Side effects / subsystem:** posts a named Wwise audio event, targeted at a resolved game
object/position (or a global default position if none is given or it fails to resolve), optionally
carrying up to two independent lists of up to 2 resolved switch/value-shaped ids each, and an
optional boolean whose own consumption inside the final post call was not independently traced past
being assembled into a combined argument block. Subsystem: audio (Wwise event posting), plus the same
named-object/position-resolution helpers `audio_play_persona_line` (§2.5) also uses. **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly for the full argument-reading chain, the table-walk helper's `t.n`-then-`pairs` fallback,
the `#PLAYER1_VEHICLE#` special case, and the mismatched-count double-push behaviour; HIGH CONFIDENCE
for the exact role of the assembled position/switch-value block in the final post call, whose own
argument (the block's address) is passed via a register the decompiler did not attribute explicitly —
does not affect the confirmed Lua-visible contract above.]**

- **Arg 2 (string, mandatory):** read via `lua_tolstring`, but the resulting pointer is never used

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a number) — `lua_pushnumber` then `return 1;`; defaults to a fixed fallback

**Body:** arg 1 is resolved through a name-lookup helper (`0x00a281a0`) shared with

`0x00a2a360`) `audio_object_post_event`'s own final post call (§2.4) uses. **[OPEN — in this
decompiled body, the local output slot this dispatch chain is meant to fill is never visibly written
to a non-zero value before being read back, i.e. this call may always yield `0` in the current build;

### 2.7 `game_peg_unload` (`0x00845650`) — 122 calls / 41 scripts

**Arguments:** 1, optional — if `lua_gettop` reports zero arguments, or the argument is nil or not a
string, or the named resource isn't found or isn't currently in one of two specific loaded states, the
function silently does nothing.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the argument, read via `lua_tolstring`, is passed to a resource-lookup helper (`0x00db3530`)
that hashes the filename (via `0x00dab330`, with a fixed constant `9000` — read as a resource-type
tag) and looks the hash up in a slot table (`0x006cf2d0`) to fetch a loaded-PEG pointer from a fixed
array (`0x029e1930`). If found, its load-state (via a small state-classifying helper, `0x00dafb60`,
returning one of 6 possible states from 3 tested flag bits) is checked; only for the two states this
classifier maps to a "fully loaded" reading is anything done: a reference-count-aware teardown routine
(`0x00dafad0` — checks the calling thread, decrements a refcount, and once it reaches zero clears
flags and releases the underlying GPU/texture resource, gated on its own flag bits) followed by a
removal from a second, separate tracking table (`0x00845080` — a fixed-size array of tracked-resource
slots, distinct from the resource system's own refcount, read as a per-Lua-binding "currently
referenced by script" list).

**Side effects / subsystem:** decrements the reference count of (and, once it reaches zero, fully
releases) a previously-loaded `.peg_pc` texture-container resource identified by filename, and removes
it from an internal per-script tracking table. Only acts when the resource is currently in one of two
specific loaded states; a no-op otherwise. Subsystem: PEG/texture resource management (the same
container format documented in `spec-texture-format.md`), specifically its Lua-binding-side reference
tracking. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, full body and call chain read.]**

### 2.8 `pop_screen` (`0x00842aa0`) — 106 calls / 45 scripts

**Arguments:** none used (same unused-`lua_gettop` pattern as §2.1/§2.6).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** calls a `__thiscall`-convention method on what reads as a UI screen-stack singleton object,
passing a literal `0` as its one explicit argument. That method's own body only proceeds if the
stack's tracked capacity and depth fields (`+0x24`/`+0x28`) are both positive, and — because the passed
argument is the literal `0` — unconditionally matches its own "expected top screen id" check (the real
comparison is `id==0 || topId==id`, and `0` here reads as a wildcard meaning "pop whatever is on top
regardless of what it is"); on a match it decrements the depth field and clears three stored
state/callback slots (`+0x148`/`+0x16c`/`+0x170`) belonging to the popped entry. A second call
(`0x00d34db0`) immediately follows, whose own body is a fixed `return 1;` with no other visible
effect in this build.

**Side effects / subsystem:** pops the current top entry off the engine's UI screen-stack singleton
unconditionally, clearing its stored state/callback slots. Subsystem: UI/screen-stack management — the
same object family `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.5 already lists `pop_screen`'s sibling `push_screen`
against. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, full body of both calls read; the screen-stack object's own class
was not independently identified beyond its field layout.]**

### 2.9 `fade_out` (`0x00a49dc0`) — 94 calls / 53 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory, 2 further optional (unusually shaped, no defensive presence check on arg
1 — read unconditionally, same as §2.3/§2.10).

- **Arg 1 (number, mandatory in practice):** a fade duration, read via `lua_tonumber`.
- **Arg 2 (table, optional):** if present and non-nil, treated as an indexed colour table — the
  function reads keys `1`, `2`, `3` from it via three independent `lua_gettable` calls (pushing the
  literal number key each time, exactly the compiled shape of `t[1]`/`t[2]`/`t[3]`) for red, green,
  and blue components respectively; any individually-nil or absent component defaults to `0.0`; if the
  whole table argument is itself absent or nil, all three default to `0.0`.
- **Arg 3 (number, optional):** a bitmask, read via `lua_tonumber` if present and non-nil; **defaults
  to the literal `3` (both bits `0x1` and `0x2` set)** if absent or nil.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the three colour components are passed, alongside a fixed literal alpha of `255`, into a
colour-state setter (`0x005d9120`, itself scaling each 0–255-range component by `1/255` before a
further internal call) — read as setting the screen-fade overlay's colour. Then, gated independently
by each bit of the (possibly-defaulted) flags argument: bit `0x1` scales the duration argument by a
fixed literal `1000.0` (a seconds→milliseconds conversion) and passes it into a helper (`0x0059f8c0`)
that manages a small phase state machine and, in the branch this call reaches, queues an internal
engine UI-command-queue message literally named `"screen_fade_do"` (read directly as a string
constant used in the command's own lookup call) carrying the scaled duration and a fixed target alpha
of `1.0` — i.e. queuing the actual timed fade-to-opaque-colour transition. Bit `0x2` independently
triggers a second, more complex helper (`0x005a0270`) that queues a *different* UI-command-queue
message (referenced only by a numeric opcode, `0x53`, not a literal name) whose own downstream effect
was not traced further in this pass.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets the engine's screen-fade overlay colour (from an optional RGB
table, defaulting to black) and, depending on the flags argument (which defaults to "both"), queues one
or both of two distinct UI/HUD command-queue messages — one a literally-named `"screen_fade_do"` timed
fade-to-opaque transition over the given duration, the other an unidentified opcode-`0x53` command.
Subsystem: UI/HUD command queue plus screen-overlay rendering state — the fade-to-a-solid-colour
counterpart implied by this cluster's `game_letterbox_fade_out` sibling name already on record in
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.5, though that is a separate, differently-named registration this task did
not decompile. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument reading (including the table-as-colour shape
and both defaults), the colour-setter call, and the `"screen_fade_do"` command-queue trigger and its
gating bit; OPEN for the identity/effect of the second, opcode-`0x53` command gated by the other bit.]** **[Resolved: see §8.13 — host-gated fade duration+flags broadcast.]**

### 2.10 `audio_conversation_play` (`0x00a3c9d0`) — 129 calls / 41 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory, read unconditionally (same no-presence-check pattern as §2.3/§2.9) — a
small numeric conversation id, read via `lua_tonumber` and truncated to a single byte.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the byte-sized id, plus a fixed literal mode value `3`, is passed to a helper (`0x006df210`)
that first attempts to queue an internal UI-command-queue message (opcode `0x51`, matching the same
numeric-opcode command-queue mechanism `fade_out`'s bit-`0x2` path uses, §2.9) carrying the id and mode
byte, gated on the queue currently being in a specific pending-write state and on the mode byte's own
bit `0x2` being set (which it always is here, being the literal `3`). Independently of whether that
queue path was taken, it also looks up whatever conversation object is currently considered "current"
(`0x006de8a0`); if one exists, marks a byte flag on it and, if a second byte flag on it is already
set, calls an interrupt/stop pair (`0x0070ba80`/`0x0046a3f0`) — read as stopping/replacing whatever
conversation is already active before the new one starts. The same mode byte's bit `0x2` additionally
triggers one more direct call (`0x008788e0`) with the conversation id, as an apparent fallback/parallel
dispatch alongside the command-queue path.

**Side effects / subsystem:** queues (and/or directly dispatches, depending on internal queue state) a
request to start the given scripted conversation by numeric id, interrupting whatever conversation is
already active if one is found. Subsystem: UI/HUD command queue plus the dialogue/conversation
subsystem already documented from the data-file side in `spec-conversation-format.md`. **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly for the full argument reading and dual queue/direct dispatch structure; OPEN for the exact
distinct roles of the command-queue path versus the direct `0x008788e0` fallback call, both of which
appear to fire under the same condition in this build.]**

### 2.11 Cross-function observations

**A shared "current position" field pair recurs across the whole audio half of this cluster.**

`audio_play_persona_line`'s own line-trigger position block (§2.5) both read the identical `+8`/`+0xc`
field pair off the value each function receives as its own first argument — i.e. off the `lua_State`
pointer itself, not a game object. Read together with `lua_gettop`'s own confirmed use of the same
`L->top`/`L->base` fields at those exact offsets (§2's method note), this is simply each function
re-reading the live Lua stack's own top/base pointers for an unrelated purpose (a coincidence of field
offset, not a real "current listener position" global) — **correcting an earlier working hypothesis
formed while first tracing §2.4/§2.5's call chains**; there is no shared listener/position global
here, only a shared struct-offset numerology between two unrelated concepts (a `lua_State`'s stack
bounds vs. whatever `0x0117f808`/`0x0117f80c` actually are, which remain a separate, real global
fallback pair — **[OPEN — `0x0117f808`/`0x0117f80c`'s own real semantics, since re-examination ruled
out the position-global reading; not re-derived further this pass.]**

**Two confirmed dual-registrations, zero coincidental ones.** §2.6 and §2.4 both show a single C
function bound under an identical name into both the gameplay (`0x00a20840`) and UI-state
(`0x00845aa0`) Lua registrars — checked directly against both raw pair-walks in each case, never
inferred from name matching alone. This is a small, real, confirmed positive answer to the task
brief's own "check both" steer for `game_is_active_input_gamepad`, generalised: at least one other
name in this exact ten-function set (`audio_object_post_event`) shares the same property, and per
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.5's own already-published overlap count (8 names total, of which these two
are members) no further dual-registration was expected or found among the remaining eight names here.

**Three distinct name-resolution families feed this cluster's audio half**, all converging on the
same real Wwise SDK entry point: the shared event/switch/category resolver `0x00462960`→`0x0046fd00`→
`AK::SoundEngine::GetIDFromString` (§2.2/§2.4/§2.5's arg-1/category reads), a separate

resource-hash family `game_peg_unload` uses (`0x00dab330`/`0x006cf2d0`) which is unrelated to audio and

behavioural oracle (real input/output vectors from actually running `audio_object_post_event` with its

uses it to locate argument 1; this one's identical prologue call is followed by no extraction at
all, consistent with a genuine zero-argument query rather than an unused/ignored argument.

accessor (`0x00681370`) before walking the member list once (comparing each entry against a
per-entry validity test, `0x00877a90`).

disassembly.]**

### 3.6 `notoriety_force_no_spawn` (`0x00a54db0`) — 234 calls / 31 scripts

**Arguments:** 2. Arg 1 mandatory string. Arg 2 mandatory boolean, read directly via
`lua_toboolean` with **no nil/absence gate** — an omitted arg 2 is read at an out-of-range stack
index, which the confirmed `lua_toboolean` body (above) resolves to "false" via the real
`luaO_nilobject` sentinel, so the practical default is still `false`, reached through Lua's own
nil-handling rather than explicit code.

**Body:** **arg 1 is not a character/vehicle name — it names a notoriety/gang track**, looked up via
`0x0094cc60` into a small numeric code (a literal `9` sentinel on lookup failure). Two resulting
codes are intercepted as hardcoded batch operations before reaching any lookup table: code `5`
toggles ten consecutive per-track flag bytes (`0x008ecda0`, each at object offset `+0x455` on ten
different track-record bases) — read as "every notoriety/gang track at once"; code `6` toggles five
of them, a narrower batch. Any other code is looked up in a small switch (`0x008ed1d0`, cases `1`,
`2`, `3`, `5`, `6` mapping to five fixed track-record base pointers — note cases `5`/`6` in this
switch are unreachable from this particular caller, since those two codes are already intercepted
by the batch branches above; the switch is shared with two other, unrelated callers where those
cases may be reachable) resolving to one specific track's own flag byte (two, for code `3`, which
sets a second, paired flag alongside the first). The `9` failure sentinel hits the switch's default

(`0x00952760` — independently confirmed in this pass to write the literal value `5` into the same
`+0xcc8` field `character_is_dead`/`0x0096f4f0` reads, and to also trigger the character's own death
animation/ragdoll and threat-list cleanup).
