### 3.18 Cross-function observations

- **Object-kind hook-array pattern:** all three `on_*` functions in this batch (`on_death` §3.2,
  `on_vehicle_destroyed` §3.3, `on_attack_performed` §3.12) plus the polymorphic `on_take_damage`
  (§3.13) register into one of (so far) three distinct per-object-kind hook-slot arrays — character
  (`+0x68`/`+0x6c`, written via `0x005e4660`), vehicle (`+0x30`/`+0x34`, via `0x00a56d50`), and an
  unidentified third kind (`+0x20`/`+0x24`, via `0x00a56d00`; **[Resolved: placed-object/mover kind, §9.21/§14.6]**) — each array holding several distinct
  named-event slots side by side (character array alone holds at least slots `0`, `4`, `6`, `8`,
  `12`(0xc — inferred by scale, not directly observed in this batch), `13`, and `18`, from the four
  functions in this batch alone). This is the concrete data structure underlying the named-hook
  family `spec-lua-bindings.md` §4/§8/§12 already established at the mechanism level; this pass adds
  the per-kind array locations and several real slot numbers, though not a full slot-number-to-
  event-name table.
- **The four/five-way object-name resolver chain** (`0x00a280c0`/`0x00a28150`/`0x00a281a0` plus the
  per-kind resolvers) is the single most-reused piece of machinery in this batch — 15 of the 17
  functions call into it for at least one argument. Its two reserved-name families (`#PLAYER#`,
  `#FOLLOWER#`/`1`/`2`/`3`) and `ai_add_enemy_target`'s own separate `#CLOSEST_PLAYER#` sentinel are
  the only non-registry ways a mission script can name a target in this cluster.
- **Debug-record tag strings are a reliable, literal cross-check for a flag setter's real-world
  name**, independent of the calling Lua function's own name: every one of the eight bit-flag
  setters this batch ~~decompiled in full~~ covered (seven decompiled in full plus `0x004e2050`, whose record branch was not re-traced, §3.4) (`0x00946190`/`0x00946300`/`0x00a7a830`/`0x00a7a9a0`/
  `0x004e2050`/`0x004e0cf0`/`0x00945eb0`/`0x00945d40`) carries its own literal, human-readable debug
  tag string (e.g. `"human_force_flagsinvulnerable"`, `"ai_force_flagscombat_disabled"`) passed to
  ~~an inactive debug/replay-log path~~ the record-and-replicate (coop/network-sync) record (live, per §3.7/§3.14/§3.16/§3.17), and in every case the tag string's own plain-English name
  matches the bit's behavioural role independently derived from its callers — a real, repeated
  agreement between two independent sources of evidence, not a single-source inference.

## 4. Vehicle/spawn-region/inventory/world-interaction cluster — 11 functions, all in the 1,014-entry gameplay table (`0x00a20840`)

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was 11 specific names from the task brief's own high
real-script-call-count list (`get_dist` 217 calls/35 scripts down to `on_vehicle_enter` 76/14). All
11 were confirmed present in the 1,014-entry gameplay array (`0x00a20840`) exactly as expected,
recovered via the same `{namePtr,funcPtr}` adjacency this document's shared Method section and
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.1/§13.2 already established: for each target name's own store
instruction inside `0x00a20840`'s body, the function-pointer store immediately following it (same
16-byte pair stride) was read directly and resolved against `.text`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly;
raw evidence at `tools/lua_gameplay_pairs11.txt`, all 11 pairs read directly with no sampling.]**
None of `continuous_spawn_stop`'s, `vehicle_is_destroyed`'s, `inv_weapon_remove_temporary`'s, or
`on_vehicle_enter`'s four function-pointer targets had previously been marked as a Ghidra
function-start (the same "valid code, not yet boundary-fixed" situation `spec-lua-bindings.md`
§13.5 already documented for roughly half of the third registrar's targets) — each was
force-disassembled and given a function boundary before decompiling; the other 7 targets were
already-defined functions.

### 4.1 Shared primitives — direct decompilation, upgrading ~~three~~ five items in the Method section above and resolving its one OPEN item

The shared Method section above (established by a concurrent pass on this same document) identified
seven stack-access primitives from their **call-site shape** alone (argument count/pattern) and
labelled ~~six~~ five of them HIGH CONFIDENCE, leaving the flag/number-extractor pair OPEN. This subsection
decompiled the primitives' own bodies directly and matched their internal logic, structurally,
against real Lua 5.1 `lapi.c` source — the same evidentiary standard `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.1
already used and had accepted for `lua_pushcclosure`/`lua_setfield`. This upgrades several items to
**CONFIRMED** and resolves the remaining OPEN pair:

- **`0x00dfde50` = real public `lua_gettop(L)`.** Its own body computes the pointer difference
  between two fields of the `lua_State` argument (at fixed offsets `+8` and `+0xc`) and right-shifts
  the byte difference by 4 — exactly the real `(L->top - L->base)` pointer-subtraction macro, divided
  by the real 16-byte Lua 5.1 value-slot stride. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe040` = real public `lua_type(L, idx)`.** Its body resolves the stack index to the
  underlying value slot, reads the slot's own type-tag field (fixed offset `+8` within the slot),
  and — critically, not just a nonzero/zero shape — returns the literal sentinel `-1` specifically
  when the resolved slot is the shared "no such value" singleton object, matching the real API's own
  `LUA_TNONE` (`-1`) special case exactly, not merely a generic tag readout. **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly, including the `-1`/`LUA_TNONE` special case, not only the tag-field readout.]**
- **`0x00dfe1e0` = real public `lua_toboolean(L, idx)`.** Its body returns `1` unless the resolved
  slot's type tag is `0` (nil) or the tag is `1` (boolean) with a stored value of `0` — the exact
  real `l_isfalse` macro Lua 5.1 uses internally, not merely a boolean-shaped wrapper. **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe160` = real public `lua_tonumber(L, idx)`.** Its body checks the resolved slot's type
  tag against the literal `3` (`LUA_TNUMBER`); if it doesn't already hold a number, it calls a
  second internal coercion helper and returns `0` on failure, else reads the numeric field directly
  — the exact real `tonumber()`-macro-plus-`luaV_tonumber()`-fallback structure, returned via the
  x87 register pair the compiler uses for a `double` return. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe210(L, idx, lenOut)` = real public `lua_tolstring(L, idx, len)`.** Its body checks the
  resolved slot's type tag against the literal `4` (`LUA_TSTRING`); on mismatch it calls an internal
  string-coercion helper, then — matching the real API's own defensive re-fetch, since a coercion can
  relocate the underlying object — re-resolves the stack-index-to-slot pointer a second time before
  reading a length field and returning a data pointer offset by a fixed `0x10`-byte string-header
  size. Every one of this section's 11 functions passes the literal `0` for `lenOut`, i.e. the real
  `lua_tostring(L, idx)` convenience macro exactly. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe3a0` = real public `lua_pushnumber(L, n)`** (not previously listed in the shared Method
  section, newly identified here because it appears in this cluster's `get_dist`). Its body writes
  the argument into the slot addressed by the `lua_State`'s own stack-top field, tags that slot `3`
  (`LUA_TNUMBER`), then advances the stack-top field by `0x10` bytes — the exact real
  `setnvalue`+`api_incr_top` expansion. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe590` = real public `lua_pushboolean(L, b)`**, settling the shared Method section's own
  "not independently distinguished from `lua_pushinteger`" caveat. Its body tags the destination slot
  `1` (`LUA_TBOOLEAN`, not `3`/`LUA_TNUMBER`, which rules out `lua_pushinteger` directly) and writes
  the argument coerced to `0`/`1`, advancing the stack-top field the same way as above — the exact
  real `setbvalue`+`api_incr_top` expansion. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **The OPEN flag/number-extractor pair is resolved.** `0x00dfe160` (`lua_tonumber`, confirmed above)
  immediately followed by a call to `0x00ea2596` is not a second, distinct stack-accessor pair —
  decompiling `0x00ea2596` itself shows it takes no `lua_State`/index argument at all; it operates
  purely on the x87 floating-point register left behind by the immediately preceding `lua_tonumber`
  call, performing a round-to-nearest double-to-64-bit-integer conversion (**[OPEN — rounding semantics: §2's method note, §3's preamble and §3.9 describe this same helper as truncation, round-half-correcting or banker's rounding; the descriptions disagree and the exact semantics is OPEN pending a re-read of `0x00ea2596`'s body. This entry is the single point of reference; other sites point here.]**). This is a shared/compiler-
  provided numeric cast helper, not a Lua C API entry point. **Resolved: this pair is simply
  `lua_tonumber(L, idx)` with its result immediately rounded to an integer — not a second Lua stack
  accessor.** **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**

### 4.2 `get_dist` (`0x00a4bdb0`) — 217 calls / 35 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings (object names) + 2 optional booleans, both default `false`,
each individually guarded by the standard nil-test idiom.

**Return:** 1 Lua value — a real `lua_pushnumber` call followed by a literal `return 1;`.

**Body:** each name string is resolved to a world position via one shared position-lookup function,
`0x00a455a0`. That function itself first tries the generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver
(`0x00a280c0` — see §4.13) and, on failure, falls back through a further chain that can reach what
reads as a coop/network remote-object position cache (`0x004dcf00`, gated by `0x009b9160`/
`0x009b9130`) for objects not resident locally, before a final fallback reads a fixed local field
directly off the resolved handle. If both names resolve, the function computes the Euclidean
distance between the two positions, with the middle (vertical) axis of the difference optionally
multiplied by `10.0` (arg 3 `true`) or zeroed out entirely (arg 4 `true` — checked after arg 3 in
the code, so it wins if both are `true`). If either name fails to resolve, the function returns the
IEEE-754 single-precision maximum representable value as a "could not compute" sentinel rather than
signalling an error.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none (a pure read). Touches the world/object-position store and,
conditionally, the coop/network remote-position cache. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument
shape, control flow, and the distance formula; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for the remote-lookup
fallback's coop/network role, since `0x00a455a0`'s own call graph was not traced past its first two
branches.]**

### 4.3 `teleport` (`0x00a60e30`) — 181 calls / 33 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings (arg 1 — the target to move; arg 2 — a destination reference) +
6 further optional arguments, each individually guarded by the standard nil-test idiom: arg 3
(boolean, default `false`), arg 4 (boolean, default `true`), args 5–7 (numbers, default `0.0` each
— read as XYZ position offsets applied on top of the destination's own position), arg 8 (boolean,
default `true`).

**Return:** none — no `lua_push*` call anywhere in the body (0 Lua values).

**Body:** arg 2 resolves through one member of the type-gated resolver family (§4.13) — the one
gating on bit `0x2` at byte offset `+0xb` of the object's type-descriptor row. Once resolved, its
stored position (3 floats at a fixed offset inside the object) is read and the three optional
numeric offsets (args 5–7) are added directly. Arg 1 (the thing being moved) is resolved separately,
through a different resolver in the same overall handle-resolution family, and a further numeric
identifier is re-derived from the resolved result before the actual move is dispatched through one
of two mutually exclusive paths depending on the resolved target's own type: a dedicated path for
one vehicle sub-category, forwarding most remaining arguments largely unchanged; or a general-purpose
apply path that additionally resets camera-, physics-, and animation-related state on the target
before moving it, and which can also funnel the change through this game's record-and-replicate
mechanism (§4.13) under some but not all conditions.

**Side effects / subsystem:** world/position, plus physics/camera/animation-state reset on the
general-apply path; conditionally network-replicated. Subsystem: world/position + character-state.
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument extraction/defaults and the two-path branch; HIGH
CONFIDENCE — inferred for the "vehicle sub-category vs. general apply" framing, since the exact
type-flag distinguishing the two paths was read but not independently named; OPEN — a position field
read from the destination object (offset `+0x4c`) that is consumed but never visibly used again in
the decompiled body, and the exact meaning of several trailing constant arguments forwarded to the
two apply calls.]**

### 4.4 `release_to_world` (`0x00a5cb10`) — 128 calls / 27 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (object name or `"#PLAYER#"`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the same name string is tried against three different members of the type-gated resolver
family (§4.13) in a fixed order — bit `0x20` at descriptor-row offset `+0xa`; then bit `0x4` at
offset `+0xb`; then bit `0x8` at offset `+0xb` — stopping at whichever succeeds first. On the FIRST
resolver's success, rather than acting on the resolved object at all, the function instead calls a
separate, zero-argument routine that walks its own global linked list (rooted off a fixed
singleton/context object) and invokes a virtual "release" method (vtable slot `+0x5c`) on every
LINKED entry whose own active-flag bit is set — a bulk "release everything currently held" call, not
scoped to the one named argument. On the SECOND or THIRD resolver's success instead, the SAME virtual
method (vtable slot `+0x5c`) is called directly and only on the one resolved object.

**Side effects / subsystem:** object-possession/ownership release. The registered name matches the
virtual method's own slot (`+0x5c`) in the two direct-call outcomes; the first resolver's global,
not-target-scoped behaviour is a genuine, slightly surprising asymmetry. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly
for the three-resolver sequence and the shared vtable-slot-`+0x5c` identity across all three
outcomes; OPEN — why the first resolver's match ignores the specific resolved object in favour of a
global bulk release, and a plain-English category label for each of the three resolvers' target
types.]**

### 4.5 `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit` (`0x00a63710`) — 116 calls / 24 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (vehicle name or `"#PLAYER#"`) + 1 optional boolean, default
`true`.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the target resolves through a dedicated object-to-vehicle-instance resolver (`0x00a281e0`):
it first checks a cached vehicle-handle field pair stored directly on the resolved base object,
falling back to a type-gated name resolution (§4.13) plus a virtual "has vehicle"/"get vehicle"
accessor pair (vtable slots `+0x68`/`+0x70`). If a vehicle instance is found, a fixed sub-offset
(`+0xc68`) inside it is computed, and that exact same sub-record pointer is passed to one of two
near-identical setter functions depending on the boolean argument (this was verified directly from
the raw instruction stream of the caller: both branches `PUSH` the identical `vehicle_instance +
0xc68` value before their respective `CALL` — an earlier decompiler rendering of one branch showing
no visible argument was a display artefact, not a real difference between the branches). Each
setter independently opens the record-and-replicate mechanism (§4.13, opcode `0x46`) and then flips
one specific bit of a byte field at offset `+0x4` of that sub-record to the boolean's value — bit
`0x40` in the "suppress" setter, bit `0x20` in the "allow" setter — when not already inside a
replicated-apply context, in which case it flips the bit directly with no re-recording.

**Side effects / subsystem:** per-vehicle NPC-exit-suppression state (two independent flag bits
inside a vehicle sub-record at `+0xc68`), network-replicated. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, including
the raw-instruction-level resolution of the apparent argument-count discrepancy between the two
branches; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for "NPC-exit suppression" as the two bits' combined role,
taken from the registered name; OPEN — which of the two bits (`0x40`/`0x20`) corresponds to which
specific sub-behaviour.]**

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (target name or `"#PLAYER#"`) + 1 optional boolean, default

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the target resolves through the generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver (`0x00a280c0`, §4.13),

using the resolved player object as an implicit method-context value. That setter, when not already

**Side effects / subsystem:** per-player restriction flag ("cannot enter/exit vehicles"),

### 4.7 `continuous_spawn_stop` (~~`0x00a21b62`~~ **`0x00a42b50`**, corrected §5.2) — 109 calls / 20 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (spawn-region name) + 1 optional boolean, default `false`.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the region name resolves through one member of the type-gated resolver family (§4.13) —
bit `0x20` at descriptor-row offset `+0xa`, the SAME resolver `release_to_world`'s first attempt
uses — then a fixed-size global table of fixed-stride records is linearly scanned for the slot whose
stored handle matches the resolved region. If found, a single stop/deactivate routine is called with
the boolean argument.

**Side effects / subsystem:** ambient continuous-spawn-region control table (shared with
`continuous_spawn_start`, §4.8). ~~**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument shape, resolver identity,
and the table-scan structure; OPEN — the exact meaning of the boolean argument, read only from the
registered function's own name and general convention, since the stop routine's own body was not

`0x00a42b50`) itself only reads `lua_gettop`/`lua_tolstring`/`lua_type`/`lua_toboolean` and forwards
the resolved name-pointer plus the raw boolean to `0x005edb90`, which resolves the name to a handle

boolean selects between virtual method slots `+0x58` and `+0x5c` of each entity's own vtable (with a
further per-entity gate, `0x00853b30(obj, 0x1e)`, that can force the `+0x58` path even when the
boolean is false). **OPEN, narrower than before but still open:** the plain-English identity of

pass) — resolving that needs the entity class's own RTTI/vtable owner identified, not just the

### 4.8 `continuous_spawn_start` (~~`0x00a21b36`~~ **`0x00a435a0`**, corrected §5.2) — 85 calls / 20 scripts

**Arguments:** up to 10 total, only arg 1 (string, spawn-region name) unconditionally read; the
remaining 9 are each individually guarded by the standard nil-test idiom: arg 2 (number rounded to
an integer, default `0` — a spawn count), arg 3 (raw number, default `0.0`, later multiplied by
`1000.0` and rounded — a respawn interval read in seconds and converted to milliseconds), arg 4
(string, default a fixed literal constant — a spawned-object/type-name filter), arg 5 (number
rounded, default `1`), arg 6 (number rounded, default `14`), arg 7 (number rounded, default `19`),
args 8–10 (each a string, default absent/`NULL`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the region name resolves through the SAME resolver `continuous_spawn_stop` uses. If a slot
for this region already exists in the shared spawn-region table (§4.7), only that slot's "active"
field is updated (a fast re-start path). Otherwise, the first empty slot in the same fixed-size table
is claimed and all ten argument values are written into that slot's parallel field arrays — count,
active flag, region handle, respawn-interval-in-milliseconds, three raw numeric fields (args 5–7),
and the type-name filter plus the two trailing optional strings fed through three dedicated
per-field setter calls. Once written, if this is a genuinely new registration (a per-slot "started"
marker byte is still clear), the region is activated via a dedicated activation call and the marker
byte is set.

**Side effects / subsystem:** the same ambient continuous-spawn-region control table
`continuous_spawn_stop` reads. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full argument-reading sequence,
every default value, and the table write/activate structure; OPEN — the concrete real-world meaning
of args 5–7 (defaults `1`/`14`/`19`) and the three optional trailing strings beyond "additional
per-region spawn parameters," since the three field-setter calls that consume them were not
decompiled past their own entry.]** Note the defaults `14`/`19` for args 6/7 reappear as literal
reset values (`0x0e`/`0x13`) inside the SAME per-slot reset routine traced in §4.7's own note above
(`0x005ec6b0`) — consistent with one shared 80-byte record shape for both functions, not
independently informative about args 5–7's own meaning.**

### 4.9 `vehicle_is_destroyed` (`0x00a65ff0`) — 97 calls / 22 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (occupant name or `"#PLAYER#"`).

**Return:** 1 Lua value (boolean-shaped) — a real `lua_pushboolean` call followed by a literal
`return 1;`.

**Body:** the argument resolves through one member of the type-gated resolver family (§4.13) — bit
`0x8` at descriptor-row offset `+0xb`, the SAME resolver `release_to_world`'s third attempt uses.
If the resolved occupant is alive, a virtual "get vehicle instance" accessor (vtable slot `+0x70` —
the SAME slot `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit`'s own resolver falls back to, §4.5) is called to obtain the
occupant's current vehicle. If a vehicle instance results, bit `0x1` of a flags field at vehicle
offset `+0x16c8` is tested and the LOGICAL NEGATION is pushed — i.e. `false` (not destroyed) is
pushed only when that bit is confirmed clear. Every other outcome (the name doesn't resolve, the
occupant isn't alive, or there is no current vehicle) pushes `true` (destroyed) as a fail-safe
default.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none (a pure query). Reads the per-vehicle "destroyed" flag (bit `0x1`
at offset `+0x16c8`), reached via the shared per-occupant vehicle accessor. **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly for the full branch structure, the shared vtable-slot-`+0x70` identity
cross-corroborated against §4.5's own resolver chain, and the exact bit tested; HIGH CONFIDENCE —
inferred that bit `0x1` means "destroyed," taken from the registered function's own name rather than
an independently confirmed field-name citation.]**

### 4.10 `inv_weapon_add_temporary` (`0x00a510c0`) — 88 calls / 23 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings (target name/`"#PLAYER#"`; weapon name) + 6 further optional

resolve, a single apply routine is called with the target, the weapon-definition record, and all six
remaining arguments; it locates or creates a per-target, per-weapon inventory-slot record and writes
an ammo count plus several flag bits into it — a "temporary grant" marker, an "auto-select after
granting" behaviour gated on one of the booleans, and a numeric tag forwarded to a separate
bookkeeping call — recording-and-replicating the change with network opcode `0x41` (§4.13) when not
already inside a replicated-apply context.

**Side effects / subsystem:** per-character weapon/ammo inventory-slot table, network-replicated.
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument shape/defaults, the shared weapon-definition table identity,

### 4.12 `on_vehicle_enter` (`0x00a588e0`) — 76 calls / 14 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, no optional arguments: arg 1 — an occupant name; arg 2 — a
vehicle/seat reference.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 2 is tried first against the generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver (`0x00a280c0`); on
success, a numeric event code (`0x16`) is posted to the occupant (arg 1) via one event-post
primitive (`0x005e4660`). If that resolver fails, arg 2 is tried against two further members of the
type-gated resolver family (§4.13) in sequence: bit `0x4` at offset `+0xb` (the SAME resolver
`release_to_world`'s second attempt uses, §4.4), then bit `0x8` at offset `+0xb` (the SAME resolver
`vehicle_is_destroyed`/`vehicle_suppress_npc_exit`'s fallback path uses, §4.5/§4.9). A match on the
first posts a different numeric event code (`0x17`) via the SAME primitive as the generic-resolver
branch; a match on the second posts a THIRD numeric code (`7`) via a DIFFERENT event-post primitive
(`0x00a56d50`), reached through a distinct implicit dispatch context than the other two (the two
posting primitives read one of two entirely different pairs of context-object fields before
dispatching).

**Side effects / subsystem:** occupant/vehicle event-notification. The three-way branch purely on how
arg 2 resolves reads as the engine distinguishing three different categories of "vehicle/seat
reference" and notifying the occupant with a different event per category. Subsystem: vehicle
occupancy / event-notification. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the three-way branch structure and
the resolver identities, cross-corroborated against §4.4's and §4.5/§4.9's own use of the same two
fallback resolvers; OPEN — the concrete real-world meaning of the three numeric event codes
(`0x16`/`0x17`/`7`) and the two distinct dispatch contexts the two posting primitives write into.]**

### 4.13 Cross-function observations

**The generic name resolver, and the `"#PLAYER#"` sentinel.** `0x00a280c0` is the base resolver
every function in this section reaches, either directly (`set_player_can_enter_exit_vehicles`,
`inv_weapon_add_temporary`, `inv_weapon_remove_temporary`, `on_vehicle_enter`'s first attempt) or
transitively (every member of the type-gated resolver family below calls it internally before
applying its own additional bit-gate). It tries the argument first as a direct name-table lookup,
and — on failure — compares it byte-for-byte against a literal `.rdata` string read directly as
`"#PLAYER#"` (8 bytes, NUL-terminated); on an exact match it resolves to the current player object
via a one-line accessor. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, including the literal sentinel string read
directly, not inferred from call-site shape.]** Every function documented in this section that
accepts an object-name string therefore transparently also accepts the literal `"#PLAYER#"` in its
place.

**The type-gated resolver family.** At least five distinct entry points share one structural body
shape (resolve via the generic resolver above, then additionally require one specific bit of a
per-object-type descriptor row — indexed by the object's own type-id byte, in a fixed global
type-descriptor table — to be set), differing only in which single bit/offset combination is
required: bit `0x2` at row offset `+0xa` (internal to the generic resolver's own numeric-handle fast
path); bit `0x2` at row offset `+0xb` (`teleport`'s destination-reference resolver, §4.3 —
most plausibly the same address as `door_open`'s own third-tier resolver, `0x005982e0`, §1.10:
`teleport`'s own body calls `0x005982e0` for this exact argument, but `0x005982e0`'s internal
bit/offset check was not independently re-derived this pass, so this cross-reference is flagged
HIGH CONFIDENCE, not re-confirmed); bit `0x4`
at row offset `+0xb` (`release_to_world` §4.4 / `on_vehicle_enter` §4.12); bit `0x8` at row offset
`+0xb` (`release_to_world` §4.4 / `vehicle_is_destroyed` §4.9 / `on_vehicle_enter` §4.12); bit `0x20`
at row offset `+0xa` (`release_to_world` §4.4 / `continuous_spawn_stop` §4.7 /
`continuous_spawn_start` §4.8). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, identical body shape read directly at
all five addresses.]** Which single plain-English category each individual bit represents (e.g.
"vehicle," "spawn region," "door") was not independently confirmed beyond the call-site pattern
above in each function's own subsection — flagged OPEN throughout rather than guessed, per this
project's own standing caution against asserting a bitfield's meaning from offset/position alone
(`WALLS.md`).

**The record-and-replicate idiom.** Four of this section's mutating paths — `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit`
(§4.5, opcode `0x46`), `set_player_can_enter_exit_vehicles` (§4.6, opcode `0x46`),
`inv_weapon_add_temporary` (§4.10, opcode `0x41`), and `teleport`'s general-apply path (§4.3, opcode
`0x17` observed) — funnel their actual state change through the identical three-call
"begin/commit/end" sequence (`0x0086f5f0`→`0x0086f110`→`0x0086eb20` in every observed instance), each
tagged with its own numeric opcode, direct confirmation that these are coop/network-synced engine
actions rather than purely local ones. `inv_weapon_remove_temporary` (§4.11) and
`continuous_spawn_stop`/`continuous_spawn_start` (§4.7/§4.8) show no trace of this same idiom in
their own bodies at this call depth — a real, confirmed asymmetry, not an assumption of uniform
replication across the whole cluster. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for all four opcode-tagged call
sequences and both non-replicated counterexamples.]**

**Recommendation for a future pass (not attempted here, out of this task's static-only scope):** a
behavioural oracle — real input/output vectors from actually running these functions — would settle
several of this section's OPEN items fastest: the plain-English category label for each of the five
type-gated resolver bits; `teleport`'s trailing constant arguments and its destination object's
unused `+0x4c` read; `on_vehicle_enter`'s three numeric event codes and two dispatch contexts; and
which of `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit`'s two flag bits (`0x40`/`0x20`) is which. This is a
recommendation only; building or running such an oracle is out of scope for this task.

## 6. Mission/trigger/notoriety/spawn cluster — 21 functions, all in the 1,014-entry gameplay table (`0x00a20840`)

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was 21 specific names from the task brief's own next-tranche list (ranks 51-150 by real script-call count; per-name counts were not supplied for this tranche the way they were for §1/§3/§4, so subsections below follow the brief's own given order rather than a locally-verified count). All 21 were confirmed present in the 1,014-entry gameplay array (`0x00a20840`) by direct lookup against `tools/lua_all_registered_1430_tagged.txt` (all 21 tagged `gameplay`) followed by a direct read of each name's own `{namePtr,funcPtr}` pair from the same full ordered walk of `0x00a20840` that §3/§4 already published (`tools/scratchpad/lua_gameplay_1014_raw_pairs.txt`) — no new array walk was needed. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; all 21 pairs read directly, not sampled.]** 13 of the 21 targets (`set_mission_author`, `notoriety_set_min_and_max`, `traffic_disable_drawbridge_area`, `notoriety_set_max`, `set_ped_density`, `notoriety_force_no_spawn_group`, `notoriety_set_min`, `spawning_pedestrians`, `set_traffic_density`, `notoriety_reset`, `waypoint_remove`, `notoriety_set_can_decay`, `mission_end_to_activity`) had not previously been marked as a Ghidra function start (the same "valid code, not yet boundary-fixed" situation §1/§3/§4 already documented for roughly half of their own targets) and were force-disassembled and given a function boundary before decompiling; the other 8 (`disable_specific_notoriety_group`, `guardian_angel_register_script_group`, `guardian_angel_unregister_script_group`, `mission_end_success`, `notoriety_set`, `spawning_vehicles`, `tutorial_start`, `mission_set_cancel_warp_location`) were already-defined functions.

Every function below opens with the same shared `lua_CFunction` prologue this document's front matter and §1/§2/§3/§4 already established and confirmed (`lua_gettop`/`lua_type`/`lua_tolstring`/`lua_toboolean`/`lua_tonumber`/`lua_pushboolean` at the same addresses) — not re-derived here, only cited.

**Read `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3.6 first (`notoriety_force_no_spawn`) — several of this cluster's functions extend or run parallel to that section's already-confirmed mechanism, cited throughout rather than re-derived.**

### 6.1 `set_mission_author` (`0x007c9f50`)

**Arguments:** none consumed. The shared prologue's `lua_gettop` call is made but its result is never used to extract anything.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the entire compiled body is the prologue call followed immediately by `return 0;` — no argument read, no push, no other engine state touched. This is a genuine, fully inert binding.

**Side effects/subsystem:** none. **A real, confirmed cross-binary finding, not limited to this one name:** this exact address is reached from at least 32 call sites project-wide, not only from this one registrar slot. One of those call sites was decompiled directly (`0x00a1fa10`, called from `0x00a1fa5a`) and turns out to be a SEPARATE, small Lua-registration table — distinct from the three registrar call sites `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13 already catalogued (`0x00a20840`/`0x008430f0`/`0x00845aa0`) — that registers five names (`script_assert`, `script_profiler_start_section`, `script_profiler_end_section`, `script_profiler_do_printout`, `script_profiler_reset`) into some Lua state, of which the four `script_profiler_*` entries are bound to this EXACT SAME address as `set_mission_author`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; the shared address and the sibling registration table's own name strings were read directly, not inferred.]** The most likely explanation is compiler/linker identical-code-folding merging several independently-written, functionally-empty stub bindings (a debug-only profiler no-op family plus this one) into one shared body — consistent with this project's own established caution (`WALLS.md`) against over-attributing meaning from a shared address alone, so this is reported as an observed fact (the address is shared, `set_mission_author` itself does nothing) rather than a claim about what the OTHER 31 call sites are for. **Flagged for the orchestrator: this `0x00a1fa10` registration site does not obviously match any of `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13's three already-counted registrar call sites and may represent additional, not-yet-inventoried registered names — worth an independent check against that spec's own total before treating the current 1,430-name count as exhaustive; not investigated further here as it is out of this task's scope.** Subsystem: none — a dead/no-op binding. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the function's own body and the shared-address fact; OPEN — why the linker folded these particular bindings together, and whether `0x00a1fa10` is a real additional registrar.]** **[Resolved (second question): `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.6 — `0x00a1fa10` is the gameplay-state bring-up routine; the 5-name table is a 4th registrar (`0x00e0ef80`), total corrected to 1,435 (later 1,490, §13.7).]**

### 6.2 `disable_specific_notoriety_group` (`0x00a47330`)

**Arguments:** 4, all mandatory, none individually nil-gated (each read directly from its stack position with no presence/type check first — the same "no nil/absence gate" idiom §3.6/§3.14 already established for a boolean argument, seen here applied to every argument in the signature). Arg 1 (string) — a notoriety GROUP name. Arg 2 (number, rounded to an integer via the shared `lua_tonumber`-then-round pair) — a tier/level index. Arg 3 (string) — the name of a specific item within that tier. Arg 4 (boolean) — the value to write.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (boolean-shaped), always pushed (either the real result or `0` on any failure path).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through a dedicated notoriety-GROUP name table (`0x008ed350` — a case-insensitive linear scan over 24 fixed name strings read directly from `.rdata`, the first being the literal `"police"`; returns a group-record pointer or null). This is a DIFFERENT resolver from §3.6's own `0x0094cc60` (which returns a small numeric code with failure sentinel `9`) — a third, independent name→record mechanism in this same notoriety family (see §6.22). If the group resolves, an unidentified zero-explicit-argument call (`0x00d21db0`) runs unconditionally, then arg 2 is range-checked against two fields on the group record (offsets `+0x3e0`/`+0x3e4`, read as a per-group minimum/maximum valid tier). If in range, the actual write is delegated to `0x008ed390`: it computes a per-tier sub-record (48 bytes per tier, from a tier-array base pointer at record offset `+0x3e8`), then linearly scans that tier's own sub-item array (32 bytes per entry, up to a per-tier count at `+0x2c`) for a case-insensitive match against arg 3 among each entry's own name field, and on a match overwrites that entry's own flag byte with arg 4, returning success/failure.

**Side effects/subsystem:** writes a named sub-item's flag byte within a specific tier of a named notoriety group. Subsystem: notoriety/gang state, extending the same family §3.6 traced. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full resolve/range-check/write chain; OPEN — the role of `0x00d21db0`, and which 24 real names populate the group table beyond the confirmed first entry `"police"`.]**

### 6.3 `notoriety_set_min_and_max` (`0x00a55b80`)

**Arguments:** 3, all mandatory, no nil-gates. Arg 1 (string) — a notoriety track name. Arg 2 and arg 3 (numbers) — a minimum and maximum value.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through `0x00605160` (see §6.22 — a THIRD, independent name resolver in this family: a case-insensitive scan across three parallel 4-entry alias-name arrays, `.rdata` strings beginning `"luchadores"`/`"brotherhood"`/`"los_carnales"`, returning a shared 0-3 index or the literal `5` on no match). Unlike `notoriety_set`/`notoriety_set_max`/`notoriety_set_min` (§6.5/§6.7/§6.11), this function explicitly checks for the `5` failure sentinel and skips the write entirely on no match. On success, `0x006082e0` is called with the resolved track code plus both numbers.

**Side effects/subsystem:** `0x006082e0` is one of a family of five track-value setters sharing one data model (§6.22) — each, when running as the sole/local co-op authority (tested via the SAME ~~co-op-session head/tail-list-empty check `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3.1 already established for `coop_is_active`~~ host check (`+0x5c`==`+0x58`, §8.27; corrected §6.22), here read off the identical accessor `0x0087ba20`), writes directly into a per-track parallel-array record; otherwise it funnels the change through the same "begin/commit/end" record-and-replicate triplet `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13 already confirmed (`0x0086f5f0`→`0x0086f110`→`0x0086eb20`), tagged here with opcode `0x3f` (a new, previously-unrecorded opcode value for that same mechanism — extends, does not contradict, §4.13's own opcode census) and an inner sub-type tag of `4` distinguishing this setter from its siblings. Subsystem: notoriety/gang per-track min/max state, network-replicated when not locally authoritative. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the resolver, the sentinel check, the co-op-authority gate, and the record-and-replicate opcode/sub-tag; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for "min/max" as the two numbers' real roles, taken from the registered name.]**

**Arguments:** 2, both mandatory, no nil-gates. Arg 1 (number, rounded) — an area index. Arg 2 (boolean) — enable/disable.

**Arguments:** 1 optional number (standard nil-gated idiom), default `3` — the same "default flag value `3`" convention already seen for `trigger_enable`'s own arg 3 (§1.1).

**Body:** the argument is passed unmodified to `0x007dd5d0`, which treats it as a bitmask-like mode selector tested by exact value: when the value is `1` or `3`, a local, non-replicated call (`0x007d6dc0`) runs; when the value is `2` or `3`, the change instead (or additionally) goes through the SAME record-and-replicate "begin/commit/end" triplet `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13 already confirmed, tagged with a further new opcode, `0x40` (extends, does not contradict, §4.13's own opcode census). Passing the default `3` (bits for both `1` and `2`) runs BOTH paths.

**Side effects/subsystem:** removes the active waypoint, via a local call, a network-replicated call, or both depending on the mode value. Subsystem: waypoint/HUD-navigation state, network-replicated on the `0x40`-opcode path. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the mode-value branch structure and the record-and-replicate opcode; OPEN — the exact real-world distinction between the two removal paths, and `0x007d6dc0`'s own internal behaviour.]**

### 6.18 `notoriety_set_can_decay` (`0x00a55110`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory boolean, no nil-gate. **Unlike every other `notoriety_set_*` function in this cluster, this one takes NO track-name argument at all — it is a single GLOBAL flag, not a per-track setting.**

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the boolean is passed, through one intermediate wrapper, to `0x006054b0`, whose own body stores the LOGICAL NEGATION of the passed value into a single global byte, `0x014a4c0f`.

**Side effects/subsystem:** sets a single global "notoriety decay suppressed" flag (stored inverted relative to the Lua-visible argument — `notoriety_set_can_decay(true)` clears the global, `notoriety_set_can_decay(false)` sets it — the same "flag stored as the negated sense of an `allow_*`-style argument" convention already confirmed for `character_allow_ragdoll`, §3.16). Subsystem: notoriety/gang global state. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the write and the polarity inversion, read directly off the stored-value expression, the same evidentiary basis §3.16 already used for its own polarity claim.]**

### 6.19 `tutorial_start` (`0x00a603f0`)

**Arguments:** up to 5. Arg 1 (string, mandatory, no gate) — a tutorial/hint identifier. Arg 2 (number, optional, standard nil-gated idiom, default `0`). Args 3-5 (booleans, each optional, standard nil-gated idiom, default `false`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through a dedicated, 210-entry (`0xd2`) fixed name table (`0x00717780`, case-insensitive linear scan, returning the matched index or `-1`) — a name space entirely separate from the notoriety-family resolvers elsewhere in this cluster. On success, the index and the four remaining arguments (with a literal `1` inserted as an internal fourth value not exposed to the Lua-visible signature) are handed to a single large dispatcher, `0x00717780`'s sibling `0x007169e0`. That dispatcher consults a matching 210-entry descriptor table (`0x0151d608`, 36 bytes per entry) and, per an entry-specific flag bit, either issues a simple prompt (`0x00715bf0`) or assembles and dispatches a richer animated/video tutorial widget (`0x00715760`→`0x007fc560`); separately, when running as the sole/local co-op authority (the same `0x0087ba20` check used throughout this cluster) and a further per-entry flag bit (or the hardcoded internal literal `1` above) permits it, the event is additionally funnelled through the SAME record-and-replicate triplet as elsewhere in this document, tagged with yet another new opcode, `0x54`.

**Side effects/subsystem:** dispatches a named tutorial/hint prompt (simple or richly-animated per a per-entry flag), optionally network-replicated. Subsystem: tutorial/HUD-hint scripting. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the resolver, the two display-style branches, and the record-and-replicate opcode; OPEN — the precise real-world meaning of args 2-5 and of several internal per-entry flag bits and threshold constants (e.g. a repeated `0xbc` split between two id ranges) were not independently re-derived past their own gating role.]**

### 6.20 `mission_end_to_activity` (`0x00a53890`)

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, no nil-gates. Arg 1 — a mission identifier. Arg 2 — an activity name.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 is gated through the SAME mission-check gate function `mission_end_failure`/`mission_end_success` use (`0x006d7240`, §1.5/§6.12). If it passes, arg 2 resolves through `0x005f4c30` — structurally identical to §6.6/§6.8's own `0x005eab60` (same outer guard, same underlying generic resolver `0x004588f0`, same shared class-descriptor table `0x02cc9900`), here testing a SIXTH catalogued bit/offset combination in this family, bit `0x4` at row offset `+0xc` (an "activity" object kind, inferred from the registered name, not independently confirmed). The resolved (or, on failure/absence/liveness-check failure via `0x00853b10`, null) handle is passed to `0x006da960`, which — itself gated by the same co-op sole-authority check as elsewhere in this cluster — when given a real handle, copies its own position-pair fields (`+8`/`+0xc`, the SAME convention as ~~§1.10/§4.3~~ §3.11/§6.12) into two globals (`0x014c8360`/`0x014c8364`) before unconditionally calling a further dispatcher, `0x006da7b0`.

**Side effects/subsystem:** transitions from a checked mission into a named activity, recording the activity object's world position into two globals along the way. Subsystem: mission-end/state-transition dispatch, sharing its gate function with `mission_end_failure`/`mission_end_success`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full resolve/gate chain and the position-pair copy; OPEN — `0x006da7b0`'s own internal behaviour.]**

### 6.21 `mission_set_cancel_warp_location` (`0x00a53900`)

**Arguments:** 2 optional strings, both standard nil-gated idiom, default absent/`NULL`.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** each argument, if present, resolves through `0x005982e0` — the SAME third-tier by-name resolver `door_open` (§1.10) uses and `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13 already flagged as "most plausibly" identical to `teleport`'s own destination resolver — gated by the shared liveness check `0x00853b10`; a resolution failure is treated the same as an absent argument. If BOTH arguments are absent (or both fail to resolve): `0x006cf050` runs, which — only while a mission is active and not in one specific game-mode state (two global checks, `0x014c8460`/`0x014c7a14`) — clears a single global (`0x014c8540`), read as a "cancel-warp override" pointer/flag. If BOTH resolve successfully: `0x006d1960` runs, gated by the SAME two global checks, and reads a field at offset `+0x4c` from EACH resolved object before combining both into a further call, `0x006d0210`. **If only one argument resolves, neither path runs at all — a genuine, confirmed partial-argument no-op.**

**Cross-section note:** the `+0x4c` field read here is the SAME field `teleport` (§4.3) reads off its own destination object but — per §4.3's own text — never visibly uses again afterward, leaving its purpose OPEN there. This function's own use of the identical field, on an object resolved through the SAME shared resolver family member (`0x005982e0`), is independent corroborating evidence that the field is real, consumed data on this object kind — it does not by itself resolve what `teleport`'s OWN body does with it, and is reported here as additional evidence for a DIFFERENT consuming function, not a resolution of §4.3's specific OPEN item.

**Side effects/subsystem:** sets (or, if both names are omitted, clears) the location the player warps to if the current mission is cancelled, keyed by two named location references. Subsystem: mission-cancel/warp state. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure, the shared resolver/liveness-check reuse, and the `+0x4c` field read; OPEN — `0x006d0210`'s own internal behaviour, and the exact real-world roles of the two arguments (e.g. "from"/"to") relative to each other.]**

### 6.22 Cross-function observations

**Three independent notoriety-track/group name-resolution mechanisms exist side by side, all converging on structurally related record types.** Besides `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3.6's own `0x0094cc60` (numeric-code resolver, failure sentinel `9`, feeding §3.6's own five-track switch `0x008ed1d0` and the batch caller of `0x008ecda0`), this cluster found two more: `0x00605160` (§6.3/§6.5/§6.7/§6.11/§6.16 — a case-insensitive scan across three parallel 4-entry `.rdata` alias-name arrays beginning `"luchadores"`/`"brotherhood"`/`"los_carnales"`, returning a shared 0-3 index or failure sentinel `5`, feeding the five value-setters `0x006079c0`/`0x00607ea0`/`0x006080d0`/`0x006082e0`/`0x00609810`) and `0x008ed350` (§6.2/§6.10 — a case-insensitive scan across 24 `.rdata` group names beginning `"police"`, returning a group-record pointer rather than a numeric code, feeding `0x008ed390`'s tier/sub-item table and, via `0x008ecda0`, the SAME `+0x455` flag byte §3.6 already confirmed on its own five hardcoded track bases). The `+0x455` flag byte and the `+0x3e0`/`+0x3e4`/`+0x3e8` tier-range fields this cluster newly read are consistent, non-overlapping offsets, HIGH CONFIDENCE (not independently proven with a shared-instance check) evidence that §3.6's track records and this cluster's group records are the same underlying object type, reached through name spaces of different granularity (a small fixed enumeration vs. a broader 24-name table) rather than being unrelated structures.

**The record-and-replicate idiom (`spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13) is confirmed to extend to three further opcode values not previously on record there** — `0x3f` (the five notoriety value-setters, §6.3/§6.5/§6.7/§6.11/§6.16, each with its own inner sub-type tag `2`-`5`), `0x40` (`waypoint_remove`, §6.17), and `0x54` (`tutorial_start`, §6.19) — all using the exact same "begin/commit/end" triplet (`0x0086f5f0`→`0x0086f110`→`0x0086eb20`) §4.13 already confirmed. This extends, and does not contradict, §4.13's own opcode census. **Cross-reference, added after review, 2026-09-29: opcode `0x40` is NOT unique to `waypoint_remove` — §9.20 (`inv_weapon_disable_all_slots`) independently uses the identical literal opcode `0x40` for a completely unrelated record. Both individual claims are correct (verified by decompile, `0x007dd5d0`/`0x007f4890` respectively); this document's opcode census is not a claim of uniqueness per name, only that each opcode's use is confirmed wherever cited.**

**A real, confirmed variation on how the record-and-replicate idiom decides "am I the sole/local authority":** §3.7/§3.14/§3.16/§3.17/§4.5/§4.6/§4.10 (already on record) gate that decision on an internal pair, `0x008ae480`/`0x008837a0`. Every record-and-replicate call site newly traced in THIS cluster (the five notoriety setters, `tutorial_start`) instead gates on the SAME accessor, `0x0087ba20`, `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3.1 already established for `coop_is_active`'s own pure query. **Correction, after independent re-verification (2026-09-29): the specific field pair this gate tests, `+0x58`/`+0x5c`, is NOT a previously-unspecified head/tail-member-list-empty pair as an earlier pass in this section claimed — it is the exact same field pair §8.27 (`game_get_is_host`) independently identifies, by the engine's own naming of that accessor, as the "is this machine the network host" check.** §3.1's own head/tail member-list-empty description covers OTHER fields of the same session-context singleton, not this pair — see §8.27 for the correct reading. This is still a genuine, checked difference between subsystems in how the same underlying "am I authoritative" decision is reached (a host-check here, vs. the internal gate pair in §3/§4's own cluster), not a contradiction of §3.7/§4.13's own findings — flagged here because the task brief asked this pass to actively check for exactly this kind of cross-section inconsistency, and the correction above is exactly such a check catching a real one.

**Two more members of the type-gated-by-name resolver family (`spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3's front matter / §4.13) were newly catalogued this pass:** bit `0x20` at descriptor-row offset `+0xa` (`0x005eab60`, used by both `guardian_angel_register_script_group` and `guardian_angel_unregister_script_group`, §6.6/§6.8) and bit `0x4` at descriptor-row offset `+0xc` (`0x005f4c30`, used by `mission_end_to_activity`, §6.20) — both structurally identical wrapper bodies over the same shared generic resolver `0x004588f0` and the same shared class-descriptor table `0x02cc9900` already established elsewhere in this document, extending that family from four/five previously-catalogued members to six (correction: `0x005eab60`/bit `0x20`@`+0xa` was already in §4.13/§4.7, so only `0x005f4c30` is newly catalogued here — five/six, one new).

**A second confirmed instance of a trivial, address-shared stub function, alongside `set_mission_author`'s own (§6.1):** `0x008ecda0` (the single-instruction `+0x455` flag-byte setter §3.6 first found and this cluster's `notoriety_force_no_spawn_group`, §6.10, also uses) has 75 callers project-wide — far more than the ones this document actually traces to notoriety state. Per this project's own standing caution against over-attributing meaning from a shared trivial-function address alone (`WALLS.md`), this document does not claim the other ~64 callers touch notoriety state; only the calls independently traced here and in §3.6 are described as such.

**`mission_end_success` (§6.12) and `mission_end_to_activity` (§6.20) both confirmed to share `mission_end_failure`'s (§1.5) own gate function `0x006d7240`**, and `mission_end_success` additionally shares that same section's final dispatch function `0x006da400`, in the same overall parameter shape (a leading flag, a text pointer, then two position pairs) — the three `mission_end_*` entry points documented across this spec so far (§1.5, §6.12, §6.20) form one coherent family built on shared plumbing, not three independent implementations.

## 7. Character/AI/combat flag-setter, hit-points, leash, and hook cluster — 32 functions, all in the 1,014-entry gameplay table (`0x00a20840`)

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was the next 32 names by real script-call count after
`spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §1–§4's top 50 (i.e. ranks 51–150's character/AI/combat share). All 32
were located directly in the 1,014-entry gameplay registrar (`0x00a20840`) via the same ordered
`{name,pointer}`-pair walk §3's own method paragraph documents (raw evidence already on disk at
`tools/scratchpad/lua_gameplay_1014_raw_pairs.txt`, re-used rather than re-run); 17 of the 32 had
never been marked as a Ghidra function start and were force-disassembled first, in a fresh disposable
project copy (`tools/gp_charai3`), using the same "force-disassemble, create function, decompile"
script pattern already on record (`AiDecForce.java`). All addresses below were cross-checked against
their own immediately-adjacent `STR:`/`FN:`/`UNK:` sequence entries before use, the same discipline
§3 applied.

**Record-and-replicate audit (explicitly requested for this cluster):** §3.7 documents a "record-
and-replicate" idiom for character/vehicle bit-flag setters — flip a bit directly only when a gate
check indicates the call is already inside a replicated-apply context, otherwise open a network
record first — and this pass was asked to check every structurally-similar simple setter in this
batch against its OWN decompiled body rather than assume uniformity. Result: the idiom is real and
present in most of the flagged names, but in **at least four genuinely different concrete shapes**,
not one:

1. **Double-gate, string-tagged** (the exact §3.7 shape): two successive gate calls (`0x008ae480`
   then `0x008837a0`); both false → open a record carrying two literal debug-tag strings (a category
   + a specific name); otherwise → flip a bit directly. Used by ~~7~~ 9 of this batch's delegates (per §7.33's list). **Note,
   added after independent review, 2026-09-29: `0x008ae480` itself is not an independent predicate —
   it does its own object-resolution/type-check first, then calls the SAME underlying function,
   `0x00884760`, variant 2's own `0x008addb0` wraps directly (with explicit arguments here, vs.
   variant 2's no-visible-argument call). The two call SHAPES are genuinely different, as described,
   but they share one bottom-line predicate — the "4 shapes" are less independent than the count
   alone suggests.**
2. **Single-gate, numeric-mode-tagged**: one gate call (`0x008addb0`, itself a thin wrapper over
   `0x00884760`); false → open a record carrying a small integer mode/sub-opcode instead of a string;
   otherwise → flip a bit or write a value directly. Used by the player-controls/movement pair and
   the hit-points setters.
3. **Single-gate, `0x008ae480`-only** (no second gate, no `0x008837a0` call at all): used only by the
   two leash functions.
4. **No gate at all — always both**: the write happens directly and unconditionally, and the record
   is opened unconditionally too, gated only by an explicit caller-supplied parameter rather than any
   internal replicated-context check. Used by `human_gravity_enable`'s delegate, and (for the record
   side only, with no direct-write alternative at all) by `set_script_animation_state`.

One flagged name, `set_attack_player_flag`, turned out to split its behaviour across **two different
flag locations** — one written unconditionally with no replication at all, the other reached only
conditionally and fully replicated via variant 1 above under a different function. Full detail is in
each function's own subsection below; §7.33 tallies the cross-cutting findings.

### 7.1 `npc_leash_remove` (`0x00a55570`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (NPC/character name).

**Return:** none.

**Body:** resolves via the generic/`#PLAYER#`-then-`#FOLLOWER#` chain (`0x00a28150`); on success,
calls `0x004e3bf0` on the resolved object. `0x004e3bf0` gates on a SINGLE check (`0x008ae480`,
compared for exact equality against `1`, variant 3 above — no second gate call anywhere in this
function): true → directly resets the character's stored leash-anchor range (a float at object
`+0x40`, reset to a fixed constant at `0x012a2d54`) and its stored leash-anchor position (a 4-float
block at `+0x30`/`+0x34`/`+0x38`/`+0x3c`, reset via a helper, `0x00da38e0`, seeded from a constant at
`0x01115d60`); false → opens a network record (opcode `0x46`, debug tags `"human_ai_data"` +
`"clear_leash"`, keyed by an object-identity pair read from the object's own `+0x610`/`+0x614`
fields, committed via `0x008ae3a0`/`0x0086f110`/`0x0086eb20`).

**Side effects / subsystem:** NPC leash/tether AI control — clears any active leash anchor.
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the call structure and both branches; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for
the real-world meaning of the reset float constants, not independently probed against real leash-
radius data.]**

`#PLAYER#` chain, not the `#FOLLOWER#` family~~ the `#PLAYER#`-then-`#FOLLOWER#` chain, §7.1/§3.4). 1 mandatory string (an action name, or the literal

a zero-argument call, `0x00ea2560`, not independently decompiled (a plausible sentinel/NaN default
rather than the plain float-constant defaults used elsewhere in this cluster).

**Return:** none.

**Body:** if arg 2 case-insensitively equals `"ALL"` (via the real public `__stricmp`), applies the

starting at `0x012e1c60` in fixed-size steps, comparing each entry's name via `__stricmp`, and returns
the matching index or, once the whole table (confirmed 70 entries, from the loop's own bound) is
exhausted, the count itself (`70`) as a "not found" sentinel. If not found, prints all 70 valid action
names to the console (one per line, via `0x004f2840` and the real public `printf`) and returns without
applying anything — a genuine, confirmed diagnostic path, not a silent no-op. If found, applies the
delay to that one action (`0x004f4ae0(object, code-and-delay-packed value, delay)`).

**Side effects / subsystem:** AI scripted-action timing/cooldown control, plus a console diagnostic on
an unrecognized action name. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the branch structure, the `"ALL"` batch

### 7.31 `set_current_hit_points` (`0x00a5f200`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string. 1 number, read unconditionally with no explicit nil/absence gate
(same un-gated shape §7.14/§7.20/§7.26/§7.29 use for booleans, applied here to a number instead —

(liveness-gated). The generic/`#FOLLOWER#`/character-resolve paths all converge on the SAME setter,

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string, resolved via `0x00a281a0`. 1 boolean read with no nil/absence

resolved value is truncated to a single byte and pushed back to Lua.

by-name lookup the "direct" naming implies exists elsewhere) and returns a small numeric handle/id.

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory numeric value, read unconditionally via the shared `lua_tonumber`-then-

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the id byte, plus a fixed literal mode value `3`, is passed to `0x006df370`. That function
(after the usual MSVC stack-protector setup, not itself program state) proceeds only if the id is not

same cluster to be the engine's own "is this machine the network host" predicate** (§8.27,

function only proceeds to its network/queue-side effect when running as host. When both that gate and

byte into it (`0x00881040`), and commits it via `0x0086f1b0`/`0x0086eb20`.

**Side effects / subsystem:** host-only, queues an opcode-`0x51` "conversation" command (subtype tag

values; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for "ends a conversation" as the queued command's real effect,

### 8.12 `camera_restrict_set_active` (`0x00a445e0`)

**Arguments:** 2. Arg 1 (boolean, mandatory, read unconditionally via `lua_toboolean` at the first
stack slot) — the active/restrict flag. Arg 2 (string, optional, standard nil-gated) — a target
name.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** a guard starts `true`, and the local setter always runs FIRST regardless of arg 2 — one of
two local setters, `0x0057a780` (clear) or `0x0057a760` (set, with a further call to `0x00d2f540` the
first time it transitions), depending on the active flag. **Corrected after independent
re-verification (2026-09-29): whether the record-and-replicate path ALSO fires depends specifically on
what arg 2 resolves to, and the "arg 2 absent" and "arg 2 resolves to current player" cases are NOT
the same case — an earlier pass in this section wrongly combined them.** Concretely:
- **arg 2 resolves (via the shared generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver `0x00a280c0`, §4.13) to the
  current player** (`0x009da4e0`, the same accessor §4.13 describes backing the `"#PLAYER#"`
  sentinel): the guard is set `false` — the local setter above runs, and the record-and-replicate
  path is skipped. **This is the only purely-local case.**
- **arg 2 is ABSENT:** the guard is NEVER set `false` — execution lands directly on the local-setter
  label, runs it, then falls through (since the guard is still `true`) straight into the
  record-and-replicate sequence below. **The local setter and the network record BOTH fire — this is
  not a local-only case.**
- **arg 2 resolves to something else (a remote/co-op target):** the local setter is skipped
  (execution never reaches its label), and only the record-and-replicate path runs.

**The record-and-replicate path** (fired for the "absent" and "remote target" cases above): opens an
opcode-`0x43` buffered record (`0x0086f5f0`), carrying a bit-packed payload built from the resolved
target and the active flag (via `0x00881110`, the bit-granularity sibling of the byte-granularity
`0x00881040` writer §8.2's family uses), and commits it the same way (`0x0086f1b0`→`0x0086eb20`).
**Note: this function does *not* use the host-check gate §8.2/§8.5/§8.18/§8.13 share** — its branch is
controlled by what the target resolves to, not by whether this machine is the host.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets a local camera-restriction flag whenever the local setter path is
reached (current-player target OR no target given); additionally queues an opcode-`0x43` command
carrying the target and the flag whenever the target is absent or a remote/co-op target — i.e. the
"absent" case does BOTH, not just the local write. Subsystem: camera state, local-vs-networked split on target
identity. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure, the shared `"#PLAYER#"` resolver
identity (citing `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13 directly, not re-derived), and the opcode/commit
call identities; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for "restriction" as the local flag's role, from the
registered name.]**

### 8.15 `hud_bar_on` (`0x00a4d9e0`)

**Arguments:** up to 6. Arg 1 (numeric, mandatory, read unconditionally) — bar-slot id. Arg 2 (string,
mandatory, read unconditionally — no presence check, the same pattern §2.3/§2.9 already flag) — a
secondary identifier string, passed straight through unresolved. Arg 3 (string, optional, standard
nil-gated, default `""`) — a label/text key. Arg 4 (number, optional, default `0.0`) — a value/percent.
Arg 5 (numeric/flag, optional, default `3`) — same flag-extractor pair as elsewhere. Arg 6
(numeric/flag, optional, default `-1`).

**Return:** none (implicit `void`, no `lua_push*` call — 0 Lua values).

**Body:** if arg 3 is non-empty, it is resolved through **the exact same three-stage localization
chain `objective_text` already established (§1.3)**: `0x00849df0` first, then (gated on the same
global at `0x026e7e68`) the secondary resolver pair `0x00604740`→`0x00604500`, then the same
`sprintf`-shaped last-resort fallback `0x00db06e0` — all three addresses identical to §1.3's own,
confirming this is one shared engine-wide text-resolution helper, not a coincidence of similar shape.

`0x0117f958`/`0x0117f95c`, read as default colour components) are all handed to `0x007edbe0`, a large
per-bar state-writer that only marks the widget "dirty" (a byte flag per changed field, at fixed
offsets of a `0x58`-byte-stride record parallel to the `0x16`-stride array §8.14/§8.16 use) when a
given field actually changed from its previous value, and additionally maintains an interpolate-toward
pair of float fields (immediate value vs. animated target, at record offsets `+0x4c`/`+0x50` relative
to the bar's own base) scaled by a further global (`0x012a2d28`) — the same "current vs. animated
target" shape §8.16's `hud_bar_set_value` also writes into, at a *different* pair of offsets
(`+0x24`/`+0x28`) on the smaller `0x16`-stride array. When flag-argument bit `0x2` is set: queues an
opcode-`0x3e` command (subtype tag `2`, payload the bar id and the flags themselves) via the same
begin/attach/commit shape as §8.2's family (`0x0086f5f0`/`0x00881110`/`0x0086f1b0`/`0x0086eb20`) — **no
host-check gate here**, purely flag-gated. When bit `0x1` is set: marks a further dirty byte and calls
`0x007eaec0` on the bar's own base record — read as an immediate local refresh/show call.

**Side effects / subsystem:** turns a HUD bar widget on with a resolved label, value, and colour
defaults; conditionally (flag-gated, not host-gated) queues an opcode-`0x3e` "HUD bar" command and/or
triggers a local refresh. Subsystem: HUD (bar widgets), sharing its localization chain verbatim with

### 8.18 `hud_set_fake_notoriety` (`0x00a4d0e0`)

**Arguments:** 3. Arg 1 (string, mandatory, unconditional) — a gang/track name. Arg 2 (boolean,

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through `0x00605160`, a case-insensitive scan (real public CRT `__stricmp`)

`"luchadores"`/`"brotherhood"`/`"los_carnales"`, slot 1 any of `"deckers"`/`"ronin"`/`"vice_kings"`,
slot 2 any of `"morningstar"`/`"samedi"`/`"rollers"`, and slot 3 accepts `"police"` under all three
names (the same literal string in each table). **These are, respectively, this series' own SR3, SR2,

written values, committed via the same local-dispatch shape as §8.2's family.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets a "fake" (debug/override) notoriety level and active flag for a
gang/track slot resolved from any of three cross-title naming conventions; host-gated, queues an
opcode-`0x40` command broadcasting the change. Subsystem: HUD (notoriety meter) / debug tooling.

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string, read unconditionally — a scene name.

### 8.23 `game_get_key_name_for_action` (`0x008422a0`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string, read unconditionally — an action name.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a string) — `lua_pushstring` (`0x00dfe420`, this document's own newly-opened
primitive, above) of an escaped/re-encoded wide-string result.

**Body:** the action name is passed to `0x005be440`, which checks it, case-insensitively, against
**the exact same two compile-time action tables `spec-tables-ui-controls.md` already fully
catalogues, at byte-identical addresses**: the 34-entry CAA (axis-action) table at `0x01122690`/
`0x01122694` (§4.2 there) and the 166-entry CBA (button-action) table at `0x01122160`/`0x01122164`
(§4.1 there). If the name matches a CBA entry with a bound (non-`-1`) value, the bound key/button code
is resolved directly through `0x005be0d0` — **the exact same low-level key-name helper
`game_get_key_name` already uses** (§2.3) — and that result wins outright. Otherwise, if the name
matched a CAA (axis) entry: axis index `0` (`CAA_CAMERA_ROTATE`) resolves to the localized tag
`"STR_THE_MOUSE"`; axis indices `2`/`3` (`CAA_WALK_FORWARD_BACKWARD`/`CAA_WALK_TURN_LEFT_RIGHT` — the
two-key WASD-style movement axes) each resolve *two* sub-action codes via `0x005be2c0`/`0x005be340`
and format them together as `"<name> / <name>"` via `0x00db0530`; any other axis index (or no match at
all) yields an empty string.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none (pure query). Resolves an action name — either a discrete bound
button/key action (via the CBA table) or a two-key/mouse movement axis (via the CAA table) — to a
localized, display-ready name string, reusing `game_get_key_name`'s own low-level resolver for the
button case. Subsystem: input (action-to-key-name resolution), directly reusing
`spec-tables-ui-controls.md`'s own already-fully-specced CBA/CAA enumerations rather than a separate
table. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure and the byte-identical CBA/CAA table
addresses, cross-cited directly against `spec-tables-ui-controls.md` §4.1/§4.2; OPEN — the exact
real-world binding behind axis indices `1` and `4`+ (not covered by any of the three handled branches,
falling through to an empty string), and `0x005be2c0`/`0x005be340`'s own bodies.]**

### 8.24 `game_peg_load_with_cb` (`0x00845510`)

**Arguments:** up to 8. Arg 1 (string, mandatory, unconditional) — a request-name/context string,
copied (bounds-checked to 64 bytes) into a per-request tracking-slot's own name field. Arg 2 (numeric,
mandatory, unconditional) — a count `N` of textures to load, used only when in the range `1..6`. Args
3 through `2+N` (each string, gated on presence via `lua_type`, breaking out early on any absent slot)
— PEG/texture filenames.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** claims the first empty slot in a small fixed per-Lua-binding request table (base
`0x02319570`, stride `0x68` bytes, bounded — the loop that finds a free slot bails out past a fixed
address ceiling rather than an explicit count field) and stamps it with the calling script's own
context (`0x00e0ceb0`'s `+0x14` field). For each of the `N` filenames: resolves it through **the exact
same resource-hash-and-lookup chain `game_peg_unload` already established** (§2.7:
`0x00db3530`→`0x00dab330(name,9000)`→`0x006cf2d0`→the PEG pointer array `0x029e1930`), then calls
`0x00dafea0` — a thread-checked (`GetCurrentThreadId` against `0x01329ea4`) load/reference-advance
routine, the direct counterpart of `game_peg_unload`'s own teardown routine `0x00dafad0` (§2.7), tested
against the same per-PEG flag bits at `+0x1e` — and, if the slot's own resolved-PEG capacity allows,
appends the resolved PEG pointer to the slot's own array. After the loop, `0x00845210` is called: it
scans **every** request slot in the same fixed table for one containing the just-resolved PEG pointer,
and only once *all* of that slot's own tracked PEGs report a "fully loaded" state (via the same 6-state
classifier `game_peg_unload` uses, `0x00dafb60`, §2.7 — states `3`/`5`) does it look up and queue a
stored command name (the slot's own `+0x28` name field) carrying the slot's own stored calling-script
context, then reset the slot's count to `0`.

**Side effects / subsystem:** loads up to 6 named PEG/texture resources into a per-request tracking
slot (reusing `game_peg_unload`'s exact hash/lookup/state-classifier chain, §2.7) and, once every PEG
in that slot has finished loading, dispatches the caller's own supplied callback name — the "with_cb"
half of the name. Subsystem: PEG/texture resource management, sharing its full resolution chain with
`game_peg_unload`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the slot-table structure, the shared hash/lookup
chain (cited directly against §2.7), and the completion-sweep/callback-dispatch structure; HIGH
CONFIDENCE — inferred that the slot's own `+0x28` field is genuinely a stored Lua callback name/token,
from the function's own registered name and the completion-gated dispatch shape, since the actual
Lua-callback invocation was not traced past the queued command lookup.]**

### 8.25 `vint_set_mouse_cursor` (`0x008456c0`)

**Arguments:** 3, all optional (standard nil-gated). Arg 1 (string, default a shared empty-string
constant at `0x0129a0e3`, verified directly against the raw bytes — the same kind of shared
empty-string default `objective_text` already uses for its own optional string arguments, §1.3,
though not confirmed to be the identical address) — a cursor name. Arg 2 (number, default `-1`). Arg 3
(number, default `-1`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the cursor name is hashed via the engine's general-purpose name hash (`0x00d9e8b0`) and
passed with args 2/3 to `0x008452e0`, which stores args 2/3 into two globals (`0x01301a08`/`0x0c` —
read as a cursor hotspot/offset pair) and special-cases the hash matching a "default cursor" sentinel
(`0x029c9964`) by substituting a different fixed hash (`0x02317c28`) and zeroing the offset pair. If
the resulting hash differs from the currently-active cursor hash (`0x02317c2c`) and a resolver
(`0x00e22490`) finds a matching cursor resource, the previous cursor resource (if any, tracked at
`0x01301a04`) is ~~released via~~ passed to `0x00754410` (a no-op stub, §18.7 — nothing is actually released) and the new hash/resource-index become current.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets the active mouse-cursor image (by name, or to a hardcoded default
sentinel name) with an optional hotspot offset, releasing the previous cursor resource. Subsystem:
UI/input (cursor rendering). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, full call chain read; empirically verified the
